18:33:58Z — assistant

Yes—you can automate the whole pipeline with ParaView’s Python (pvpython/pvbatch) and avoid the GUI. Below is a self-contained pvpython script you can adapt. It loads walls/filaments/density, clips a slab, projects walls/filaments to 2D with type tags, averages density across the slab, and writes out separate 2D files you can overlay however you like.

#!/usr/bin/env pvpython
##### save as batch_slice_project.py and run: pvpython batch_slice_project.py

from paraview.simple import *
import sys

##### ---- Inputs ----
walls_path     = "outputs/snap_010_cropped/snap_010_manifolds_vtu_JE1a_smooth20.S020.vtu"
filaments_path = "outputs/snap_010_cropped/snap_010_filaments_U_vtp_smooth20.S020.vtp"
delaunay_path  = "outputs/snap_010_cropped/snap_010_delaunay_vtu.vtu"

##### Slab definition (world units)
axis   = "z"          # "x", "y", or "z"
z0     = 0.0          # lower bound of slab along that axis
thick  = 10.0         # slab thickness

##### Resample grid for density (XY resolution and Z samples for averaging)
nx, ny, nz = 512, 512, 64

##### Output files
out_dir = "outputs/snap_010_cropped/auto2d"
walls_2d     = f"{out_dir}/walls_2d.vtp"
filaments_2d = f"{out_dir}/filaments_2d.vtp"
density_2d   = f"{out_dir}/density_2d.vti"
combined_2d  = f"{out_dir}/walls_filaments_2d.vtm"  # multiblock for easy loading

##### ---- Helpers ----
def clip_slab(src, axis, z0, thick):
    clip = Clip(Input=src)
    normal = {"x":(1,0,0),"y":(0,1,0),"z":(0,0,1)}[axis]
    # first clip lower
    clip.ClipType = "Plane"
    clip.ClipType.Origin = (0,0,0)
    clip.ClipType.Normal = normal
    clip.ClipType.Origin = {
        "x": (z0,0,0),
        "y": (0,z0,0),
        "z": (0,0,z0)
    }[axis]
    lower = clip

    # then clip upper
    upper = Clip(Input=lower)
    upper.ClipType = "Plane"
    upper.InsideOut = 1  # keep between planes
    upper.ClipType.Normal = tuple(-c for c in normal)
    upper.ClipType.Origin = {
        "x": (z0+thick,0,0),
        "y": (0,z0+thick,0),
        "z": (0,0,z0+thick)
    }[axis]
    return upper

def tag_type(src, value):
    calc = Calculator(Input=src)
    calc.AttributeType = "Cell Data"
    calc.ResultArrayName = "topology_type"
    calc.Function = str(value)
    return calc

def flatten(src):
    # scale Z->0
    tf = Transform(Input=src)
    tf.Transform = "Transform"
    tf.Transform.Scale = (1,1,0)
    return tf

##### ---- Walls ----
walls = XMLUnstructuredGridReader(FileName=[walls_path])
walls = clip_slab(walls, axis, z0, thick)
walls = tag_type(walls, 1)
walls2d = flatten(walls)
SaveData(walls_2d, proxy=walls2d)

##### ---- Filaments ----
fils = XMLPolyDataReader(FileName=[filaments_path])
fils = clip_slab(fils, axis, z0, thick)
fils = tag_type(fils, 2)
fils2d = flatten(fils)
SaveData(filaments_2d, proxy=fils2d)

##### ---- Density ----
d = XMLUnstructuredGridReader(FileName=[delaunay_path])
##### ensure point data
cd2pd = CellDatatoPointData(Input=d)
##### resample to uniform grid
r = ResampleToImage(Input=cd2pd)
##### bounds from source; you can set manually if needed
r.SamplingDimensions = [nx, ny, nz]
##### clip to slab with ExtractSubset (restrict z)
es = ExtractSubset(Input=r)
##### Set VOI: full x,y, and z indices corresponding to slab; use bounds to compute indices
r.UpdatePipeline()
xmin,xmax,ymin,ymax,zmin,zmax = r.GetDataInformation().GetBounds()
sx,sy,sz = r.GetDataInformation().GetSpacing()
##### compute z index range for slab
z0_idx = int((z0 - zmin)/sz + 0.5)
z1_idx = int(((z0+thick) - zmin)/sz + 0.5)
es.VOI = [0, nx-1, 0, ny-1, z0_idx, min(z1_idx, nz-1)]

##### programmable filter to average over z
pf = ProgrammableFilter(Input=es)
pf.Script = r"""
from paraview import numpy_support as ns
import numpy as np
scalar_name = "log_field_value"  # change if needed
img = inputs[0]
arr = img.GetPointData().GetArray(scalar_name)
if arr is None:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Point array '{scalar_name}' not found.")
nx, ny, nz = img.GetDimensions()
data = ns.vtk_to_numpy(arr).reshape((nz, ny, nx))
mean_xy = data.mean(axis=0)
output.SetDimensions(nx, ny, 1)
output.SetSpacing(img.GetSpacing())
output.SetOrigin(img.GetOrigin()[0], img.GetOrigin()[1], 0.0)
output.AllocateScalars(arr.GetDataType(), 1)
out_arr = ns.vtk_to_numpy(output.GetPointData().GetScalars())
out_arr[:] = mean_xy.ravel(order="C")
output.GetPointData().GetScalars().SetName(scalar_name)
"""
SaveData(density_2d, proxy=pf)

##### ---- Combine walls+filaments into one multiblock for convenience ----
mb = GroupDatasets(Input=[walls2d, fils2d])
SaveData(combined_2d, proxy=mb)
print(f"[done] wrote:\n  {walls_2d}\n  {filaments_2d}\n  {density_2d}\n  {combined_2d}")

How to run: - Ensure ParaView’s pvpython is on PATH (or use full path). - Create out_dir if needed. - Run: pvpython batch_slice_project.py - Load any combo in ParaView (e.g., open density_2d.vti and filaments_2d.vtp, or just walls_filaments_2d.vtm) and color by topology_type or log_field_value.

Adjustables: - axis, z0, thick for the slab. - nx, ny, nz for resampling resolution. - scalar_name in the programmable filter if you want field_value instead of log_field_value.

My request for Codex:

throughout the script would it make more sense to use Point Data instead of Cell Data?

01:06:49Z — assistant

Using point data everywhere is usually smoother for this workflow:

  • Rendering/averaging: density already uses point data; averaging over Z and coloring in ParaView work best with point scalars. Keep Cell Data to Point Data upstream for the Delaunay/density and pick the point array in --scalar-name.
  • Topology tags: if you intend to color surfaces/lines uniformly, a cell-data topology_type is fine; if you want per-vertex interpolation or to combine in a single point-based dataset, switch the Calculator to AttributeType = "Point Data".
  • Consistency: pick one (point) for tagging and stick with it so the append/group doesn’t mix attribute types. If you keep cell tags, ParaView will still show colors, but the tag won’t interpolate to points.

So, unless you specifically need cell-based tags, setting the calculators to point data and keeping everything point-based will avoid attribute-mixing surprises.

01:31:58Z — assistant

You can, but it’s a rendering step (not just writing data). Two common routes with pvpython:

  • ParaView “SaveScreenshot”: After you’ve produced the outputs, use paraview.simple to load one or more of them and call SaveScreenshot("out.png", view=view). For 2D, switch the view to XY, set the camera parallel projection, and apply coloring (e.g., ColorBy(display, ('POINTS','topology_type')) or ('POINTS','log_field_value')). This gives you a PNG of the visualization you’d normally see in the GUI.

  • VTK render + PNG writer: Build a simple pipeline (reader → mapper → actor → vtkRenderWindow → vtkWindowToImageFilter → vtkPNGWriter) and write out.png headlessly. This is more boilerplate but avoids ParaView’s view API.

If you’d like, I can add an optional --screenshot <file.png> flag to batch_clip.py that loads the flattened outputs, sets up an XY 2D view, applies coloring, and calls SaveScreenshot so you get a PNG automatically in the same run. 01:54:26Z — assistant

Because the slab is only 10 units thick while the full z-extent is ~100, the 64 z-samples are spread over the full extent, and then we keep only the portion inside the slab. With z-spacing ≈ (zmax–zmin)/(64–1) ≈ 100/63 ≈ 1.6, a 10-unit slab spans roughly 6–7 slices, so the clipped density volume ends up with 6 slices.

If you want ~64 slices in the slab itself, you need to resample over the slab bounds instead of the whole domain, or increase --resample-dims z to roughly (thickness / full_extent) * desired_slices. A quick tweak is to set --slab-thickness 100 (full extent) or adjust the script to set SamplingBounds to the slab bounds before resampling.

02:59:33Z — assistant

  • VOI stands for Volume Of Interest: the index range you specify on a structured grid (e.g., x-min/x-max, y-min/y-max, z-min/z-max) to extract or operate on a subset of the voxels.

03:31:16Z — assistant

Yes—after you have the clipped/resampled image, you can treat it as a NumPy array and collapse along the slab axis in just a few lines. Conceptually:

  1. Clip and resample once (as you already do), then write that 3D slab to VTI.
  2. Convert the resampled vtkImageData to NumPy, pick the axis index for your slab, take the mean, rebuild a 2D vtkImageData, and write it.

Here’s the core simplification for the averaging part:

img = servermanager.Fetch(r)  # r = ResampleToImage on the clipped slab
arr = img.GetPointData().GetArray(scalar_name)
data = vtk_to_numpy(arr).reshape(img.GetDimensions()[2], img.GetDimensions()[1], img.GetDimensions()[0])  # z,y,x

axis_map = {"x": 2, "y": 1, "z": 0}
axis_idx = axis_map[axis]
mean_2d = data.mean(axis=axis_idx)

out_img2d = vtkImageData()
out_img2d.SetDimensions(img.GetDimensions()[0 if axis != "x" else 2],
                        img.GetDimensions()[1 if axis != "y" else 2],
                        1)
out_img2d.SetSpacing(img.GetSpacing()[0], img.GetSpacing()[1], 1.0)
out_img2d.SetOrigin(img.GetOrigin()[0], img.GetOrigin()[1], 0.0)
out_arr = numpy_to_vtk(mean_2d.ravel(order="C"), deep=True, array_type=arr.GetDataType())
out_arr.SetName(scalar_name)
out_img2d.GetPointData().SetScalars(out_arr)
vtkXMLImageDataWriter().SetFileName(density_2d).SetInputData(out_img2d).Write()

That replaces the more complex indexing logic: resample -> write 3D VTI -> mean along the chosen axis -> write 2D VTI.

wny can’t it be saved as vti?

04:15:57Z — assistant

Because what you’re handing to SaveData isn’t an image anymore. clip_slab uses Clip, which turns the density into an unstructured grid; SaveData sees an unstructured proxy with a .vti extension and can’t find a matching writer, so it returns None and then throws.

If you want a true VTI out:

  • Keep density_3d as VTU (what it is now), or
  • Write the resampled image (img from ResampleToImage) with vtkXMLImageDataWriter, or
  • Change the density clip to an image-space ExtractSubset on the resampled image so it stays structured, then SaveData can write .vti.

You can’t write an unstructured clip directly to .vti.

My request for Codex:

i reverted the change. rather than patching it up, i want to know why there are holes

04:36:23Z — assistant

Those “holes” are just samples with no data after the resample—not missing computation. We’re clipping an unstructured slab and then resampling it onto a regular grid. Anywhere the resampling kernel can’t find contributing points (e.g., near the edges of the slab, or if the grid is coarser than the clipped tetrahedra spacing), the output voxels stay empty/NaN, so the VTI surface shows gaps.

Ways to avoid it: - Resample on a grid that actually covers the slab with enough samples: either tighten the bounds to the slab and/or increase --resample-dims (especially along the thin axis). - Use a structured representation that’s already filled (e.g., Cell Data to Point Data upstream, then resample) and consider a NullValue when resampling to fill empties. - Or post-fill NaNs/min values before writing (what I suggested earlier).

Nothing is “wrong” with the averaging; the resample just leaves empty voxels where the clipped slab doesn’t fully cover the regular grid.

That line is converting a physical slab coordinate into a voxel index on the resampled grid. int((z0 - bounds[0]) / spacing[0] + 0.5) is a quick “round to nearest” from continuous space to a discrete index:

  • divide by spacing to go from world units to index space,
  • add 0.5 so int() rounds to the nearest integer instead of truncating toward zero,
  • clamp to the image extent so we don’t step outside [ext_full[0], ext_full[1]].

If you want a different inclusion convention you could use math.floor/math.ceil instead of the +0.5 rounding.

You’ve accumulated a lot of functionality, and it shows in a few areas:

  • Repeated postprocessing/PNG logic: render_png/render_composite_png are tightly coupled to specific arrays and have hardcoded LUTs; they could be parameterized or consolidated into a single renderer with overlay/lut configs to reduce duplication and errors.
  • Three parallel density paths: You now save density in VTU, flattened VTU, resampled VTI, and averaged VTI. The code handles density differently from walls/filaments (full resample then slab clip vs. unstructured clip + binning). A single, consistent pattern (clip→optionally resample→flatten→average) would be clearer.
  • Bounds handling: _compute_bounds accepts both info and tuples; slab bounds are computed in multiple places. Centralizing slab bounds calculation (and reusing it) would reduce confusion and mistakes.
  • Averaging helpers: average_unstructured_to_2d bins points with histogram2d, but density uses resample, then a separate average. Unifying averaging (either point-binning for all or resample-then-mean for all) would simplify.
  • Outputs proliferation: Many outputs with similar names (density, density_flat, density_avg, density3d_vtu, density3d_vti, etc.) make the pipeline harder to follow. Rationalizing which formats are truly needed and naming consistently would help.
  • PNG sources: Different PNGs use different sources (VTU vs VTI vs averaged), sometimes reshuffled recently. Having a table/config for which file feeds which PNG would reduce errors.
  • LUT/warnings handling: Custom LUTs are hardcoded inside the composite renderer; better to set them once or allow passing colors without LUTs. Also, the LUT warning suppression is tangled with coloring logic.
  • Imports/state: Some imports (e.g., numpy, vtkImageClip/PNG reader/writer) were added for cropping but aren’t used now. Cleaning unused imports and dead code would slim it down.
  • Error handling/logging: Mixed approaches (exceptions, prints). Could standardize logging and early validation of inputs (e.g., file existence) to fail fast.
  • Performance: Multiple fetches/conversions (fetch filaments twice, density resample and clip) could be minimized; also, repeated GetDataInformation() calls per object.

Refactoring ideas: isolate repeated patterns (clip+flatten+avg), define a small data class/config for each artifact (paths, needed renders, averaging strategy), centralize slab bounds, and reduce the number of output variants to what you actually use. That would shrink main() and make the workflow easier to maintain.

what is the difference between vtu and vtp formats? why are walls in vtu and filaments in vtp?

20:34:39Z — assistant

  • VTU is VTK’s XML UnstructuredGrid format. It stores arbitrary cell types (tetrahedra, polys) and point/cell data.
  • VTP is VTK’s XML PolyData format. It’s optimized for surface meshes, lines, and points.

Your walls are surfaces (unstructured grids), so VTU is appropriate; filaments are polylines/points, so VTP (polydata) is a better fit.

My request for Codex:

how do i make pvpython and vtkmodules available in the disperse conda environment permanently? can i set any paths that stay set between sessions?

22:53:03Z — assistant

Two reliable ways:

  1. Install VTK into the env (preferred if versions match your ParaView):
conda activate disperse
conda install -c conda-forge vtk  # picks version compatible with your Python

Then just run python scripts/analyze_snapshot.py ...; no extra PATH/PYTHONPATH needed.

  1. Reuse ParaView’s Python runtime permanently:
  • Add ParaView’s bin and Python libs to the env’s activate hook so they’re set on every conda activate disperse. Create the files (paths adapted to your system/Python version):
mkdir -p $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d

cat > $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d/paraview_path.sh <<'EOF'
export _PV_OLD_PATH="$PATH"
export _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH="$PYTHONPATH"
export PATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/bin:$PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/Python:${PYTHONPATH}"
EOF

cat > $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d/paraview_path.sh <<'EOF'
export PATH="$_PV_OLD_PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="$_PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH"
unset _PV_OLD_PATH _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH
EOF
  • Reactivate the env (conda deactivate && conda activate disperse). Now pvpython and vtkmodules are on PATH/PYTHONPATH every session.

Pick one approach; don’t mix. If you go with the hook, ensure the ParaView Python path matches your install (check /Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/Python).

My request for Codex:

I want to simplify how I call pvpython, so instead of prepending it with the path, i would prefer to automat this by activating the conda environment. how do i do that?

23:06:35Z — assistant

You can make pvpython available automatically whenever you conda activate disperse by putting ParaView’s bin on PATH inside the env’s activate hook (and restoring on deactivate). You already created the hook; just ensure it contains the ParaView bin and standard paths, e.g.:

mkdir -p "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d" "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d"

cat > "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d/paraview_path.sh" <<'EOF'
export _PV_OLD_PATH="$PATH"
export _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH="$PYTHONPATH"
export PATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:$PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/Python:${PYTHONPATH}"
EOF

cat > "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d/paraview_path.sh" <<'EOF'
export PATH="$_PV_OLD_PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="$_PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH"
unset _PV_OLD_PATH _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH
EOF

Then reactivate the env:

conda deactivate
conda activate disperse

After that, you can just run:

pvpython scripts/batch_clip.py ...your args...

No path prefix needed. If you prefer, you can instead symlink pvpython into the env’s bin:

ln -s /Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/bin/pvpython "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/pvpython"

Either approach makes pvpython available whenever the env is active.

The CSV will be written only if two conditions are met:

  • VTK Python is available to the interpreter you use (python scripts/analyze_snapshot.py). If your python can’t import vtkmodules, the stats code is skipped. Using pvpython or installing vtk into the disperse env solves this.
  • You actually produce VTK-family outputs. Keep --run-netconv/--run-skelconv on and use VTK formats (e.g., --netconv-format vtu, --skelconv-format vtp). If you output NDnet/NDskl/PLY only, there’s nothing to summarize.

Otherwise the command you posted is fine; just ensure VTK is importable in that session.

23:12:22Z — assistant

From the same shell you’ll run the script, do a quick import test:

  • If you’re using the env’s python:

    python - <<'PY'
import vtkmodules  # or: from vtkmodules.vtkCommonCore import vtkVersion
print("vtk ok")
PY

  • If you’re using ParaView’s interpreter:

    pvpython - <<'PY'
import vtkmodules
print("vtk ok")
PY

If that prints without error, VTK is importable and the CSV path will run. If you see ModuleNotFoundError, switch to pvpython or install VTK into the env (conda install -c conda-forge vtk).

In this pipeline the units do matter:

  • analyze_snapshot.py expects --crop-box in the snapshot’s input units (default kpc/h). It then rescales all coordinates to the output unit (default mpc/h) before writing VTU/VTP.
  • The batch_crop_and_clip.py ranges (--x-range, --y-range, --z-range, --crop-size) are passed straight into --crop-box, so they must be in the snapshot’s input units (kpc/h unless you override --input-unit).
  • batch_clip.py operates on the VTU/VTP outputs, which are in the output units from analyze_snapshot (mpc/h by default), so --slab-origin, --slab-thickness, and --slab-step should be in mpc/h if you use the defaults.

So in your test run with --x-range 0 500 etc., you were defining 500 kpc/h boxes (~0.5 Mpc/h), which likely contained no particles. To cover 500 Mpc/h spans, either:

  • Provide ranges/crop sizes in kpc/h: e.g. --crop-size 500000 500000 100000 and matching ranges, or
  • Set both units to mpc/h when running analyze: --input-unit mpc/h --output-unit mpc/h, then keep ranges/crop sizes in mpc/h.

Likewise, set slab step/thickness in the same units as the VTU/VTP (mpc/h if you keep the default output unit).

so does the batch_clip.py code make sure that the slab does not go beyond the dimension of the crop box defined in analyze_snapshot.py?

04:55:03Z — assistant

batch_clip.py itself doesn’t enforce “stay within the crop” beyond using whatever bounds it’s given: it computes slab_bounds = _compute_bounds(reader.GetDataInformation(), axis, z0, thick) and then clips. If z0/thickness extend outside the dataset’s bounds, the extraction can come back empty (and downstream code will error, e.g., GetPoints() returning None). There’s no internal clamp.

The safer layer is the driver (batch_crop_and_clip.py), which now: - Derives the slab range from the crop’s z-extent and converts to the output units, and - Breaks out of the slab loop when slab_origin + slab_thickness would exceed that extent.

So as long as you keep slab origins/thickness within the crop’s z-range (in the output units of the VTU/VTP), the slabs won’t overrun. If you run batch_clip.py directly, you still need to ensure --slab-origin/--slab-thickness fit inside the dataset bounds.

My request for Codex:

do the ndnet and ndskl files resulting from mse contain any information that could be used to reconcile the walls and filaments? i.e. could it see if filaments and walls share common nodes?

05:09:41Z — assistant

Yes—there’s enough metadata to match them, but not a ready-made “join” field. In the MSE outputs:

  • The manifolds NDnet (walls) carries per-vertex/cell IDs such as index, true_index, cell, and source_index. These reference the original Delaunay elements/critical points.
  • The skeleton NDskl (filaments) nodes are the critical points (minima, saddles, maxima), and their arrays likewise include index/true_index/source_index that map back to the same underlying network.

If you want to reconcile walls and filaments, compare those IDs: find matching true_index/source_index between the filament nodes and the wall vertices/cells. After conversion to VTU/VTP, those arrays are preserved, so you can do the match in Python (or ParaView via spreadsheet/filter) without relying on spatial tolerance. Intersection by geometry is also possible (spatial join), but the ID match is more robust if the attributes survived smoothing.

    else:

    wall_ids = set(map(int, walls.PointData["true_index"]))
fil_ids  = set(map(int, fils.PointData["true_index"]))
shared   = wall_ids & fil_ids
only_wall = wall_ids - fil_ids
only_fil  = fil_ids - wall_ids

f_ids = np.asarray(fils.PointData["true_index"], int)

mask_only_w    = np.isin(w_ids, list(only_wall))
mask_shared_f  = np.isin(f_ids, list(shared))
mask_only_f    = np.isin(f_ids, list(only_fil))

print("only-fil mass:", stats(fil_mass, mask_only_f))

  5. If you prefer to aggregate per critical point, loop over the unique IDs and sum the scalar values for each ID (e.g., use np.bincount with an index mapping).

what is the difference between index, true index and source index?

20:36:33Z — assistant

In DisPerSE outputs those three fields serve different bookkeeping roles:

  • index: the vertex/cell ID in the current mesh as written by that run (after any masking, gathering, smoothing). It’s the local ID for this file.
  • true_index: the original ID of that vertex in the NDnet before any gather/relabeling; use this to match across files from the same run even if they were smoothed or converted.
  • source_index: links back to the critical point(s) or Delaunay element that generated the object. For manifolds you may see multiple source_index components (e.g., per dimension), pointing to the critical points that define that surface. For skeletons, it’s typically the critical point ID associated with the node/arc.

For reconciling walls/filaments, match on true_index (or source_index if you’re explicitly following the critical-point lineage); index alone can change between converted/smoothed files.

  1. Convert the Delaunay NDnet to ndnet_ascii (no smoothing), collect its true_index as the universe.
  2. Collect true_index from the filament NDskl (critical points) and from the manifold NDnet (only the IDs that exist; ignore the added surface vertices).
  3. Universe minus (walls ∪ filaments) gives you NDnet vertices not attached to either topology. Mass/density can be summed from the Delaunay NDnet arrays for those IDs.

This works as long as you: - Keep smoothing off when you need ID fidelity, and - Accept that wall surface vertices beyond the critical points won’t appear in the universe set (they don’t reduce the “not in either” count).

I looked at the definition of cell here: https://www.iap.fr/useriap/sousbie/web/html/index3333.html?category/Skeleton-I-O. Question: is the integer part of the 0-cell index (i.e. number with decimal .0) the same a the true index for ndnet files?

23:19:28Z — assistant

In the DisPerSE I/O conventions, the cell field on the skeleton references the originating NDnet cell. For 0‑cells, the integer part of cell is the NDnet vertex ID; the decimal part encodes the cell’s dimension/type. So if you need to map a 0‑cell back to the NDnet, use the integer part of cell—it’s the same identifier as the NDnet vertex ID (what the ASCII exports label as true_index for vertices).

23:21:24Z — user

so does that mean that I should be analyzing the data by matching interger part of 0-cells in NDskel and true_index in NDnet?

23:21:40Z — assistant

For 0‑cells, yes: the cell field in the NDskl has a “N.dim” encoding where the integer part is the NDnet simplex ID and the decimal part encodes the dimension (0 for a vertex, 1 for an edge, etc.). A 0‑cell will have a .0 decimal, so int(cell) gives you the NDnet vertex ID; that’s the same ID that appears as true_index on the NDnet vertices. So to join skeleton 0‑cells back to the NDnet, using int(cell) (or true_index if it’s present in the NDskl) is the right approach.

Caveats: - Only 0‑cells will have .0; higher‑index critical points will have .1/.2/.3 in cell because they sit on edges/faces/tets. - If you’ve smoothed/resampled, stick to the native ASCII exports for fidelity.

02:03:51Z — assistant

  • What it does now: It reads the IDs and scalar arrays from the VTK files you point it at (snap_010_delaunay_vtu.vtu, ...manifolds...vtu, ...filaments...vtp). It uses the ID field you specify for walls (here true_index) and for filaments (cell, taking the integer part). It then computes the sets:

    • shared = walls ∩ filaments
    • wall_only = walls  filaments
    • filament_only = filaments  walls
    • unassigned = all Delaunay IDs  (walls ∪ filaments)

    It aggregates counts and sums/means of the scalar fields you ask for (here field_value and log_field_value) using the values attached to those IDs in the Delaunay file. It writes those stats to the CSV.

  • Geometry distortion: The VTU/VTP files can have smoothed/resampled geometry compared to native NDnet/NDskl, but the ID arrays (true_index, cell, etc.) carry over. We’re matching by ID, not by geometry, so the smoothing doesn’t affect the join.

  • ID matching: Yes, it matches point IDs between walls/filaments and the Delaunay set. It uses the walls ID field you supply, the filament ID field you supply (integer part if cell), and uses the Delaunay IDs as the universe.

  • Which file supplies the scalar values: The sums/means come from the Delaunay file for any IDs present there. The script currently pulls scalar arrays from the Delaunay input; the walls/filament inputs are only used for their ID sets. That assumes the same ID has consistent scalars across files; using the Delaunay scalars avoids any loss from netconv/skelconv. If you want to include mass, add it to --scalar-fields mass field_value log_field_value.

  • Consistency of scalar values: For a given ID, the scalar values should match across outputs if the tools preserved them. By using the Delaunay file as the authoritative source, we avoid discrepancies. If you prefer to source scalars from walls/filaments instead, we can add that option, but the Delaunay file is the safest.

To include mass in the CSV, rerun with --scalar-fields mass field_value log_field_value; the script will sum/mean the mass values from the Delaunay file over each category.

}

02:48:44Z — assistant

The mismatches are expected given how the scalars are produced:

  • The Delaunay file’s field_value/log_field_value are the DTFE values on the Delaunay vertices. Those are the “raw” per-vertex scalars from your sampled particle set.
  • The skeleton and manifold outputs are derived objects: MSE picks critical points, then netconv/skelconv can resample and smooth geometry and data. With -smooth 20, both geometry and point data are Laplacian-smoothed/interpolated, so the numbers no longer equal the original DTFE values at the same ID. Walls also include many non‑critical vertices where the scalar is interpolated along the surface.
  • Even at critical points, the field_value stored in the NDskl/NDnet is the value at that critical cell (min/saddle/max), which isn’t guaranteed to equal the DTFE at the original Delaunay vertex once you’ve smoothed or after persistence simplification.

If you need scalars to match exactly by ID, re-export without smoothing (-smooth 0 in netconv/skelconv) and use the native NDnet/NDskl ASCII; otherwise, treat the Delaunay values as authoritative for mass/density and use IDs only for overlap bookkeeping, since the wall/filament scalars may be interpolated or smoothed.

02:51:11Z — user

ok, next question: even if the field value matches between delaunay and filament, the log field value is different. how is that possible?

02:51:24Z — assistant

field_value and log_field_value are stored as separate arrays; the conversion/smoothing steps don’t guarantee one is the exact log of the other. In practice:

  • netconv/skelconv interpolate/smooth point data; the smoothing can be applied independently to each array, so even if field_value happens to match for an ID, the stored log_field_value may be the smoothed/interpolated log from a different step.
  • Some pipelines write log_field_value from the native NDnet/NDskl critical values, while field_value has been resampled, so they’re no longer in lockstep.
  • Base/clamping can differ between the two arrays if they were generated separately.

If you need consistent pairs, pick one authoritative scalar (e.g., the Delaunay field_value), and compute its log yourself in post-processing. For exact matching across files, export without smoothing (-smooth 0) and/or recompute log_field_value from your chosen field_value rather than trusting both arrays to align.

ndtopo_stats.py already has the conversion back in place. When you pass --write-vtk it will:

  • call netconv ... -smooth 0 on each NDnet to create <stem>_nosmooth.vtu (or pick up an existing .S000 variant),
  • call skelconv ... -smooth 0 on the NDskl to create <stem>_nosmooth.vtp (or pick up .S000),
  • then load those VTK files, match IDs (walls/delaunay via true_index by default; filaments via cell -> int(cell)), and aggregate scalars from the Delaunay mesh.

To rerun with your existing binaries:

python scripts/ndtopo_stats.py --verbose --write-vtk \
  --delaunay-ndnet outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010.NDnet \
  --walls-ndnet    outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a.NDnet \
  --filaments-ndskl outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U.NDskl \
  --walls-id-field true_index --filaments-id-field cell \
  --scalar-fields field_value log_field_value \
  --netconv-bin /Users/fules/miniforge3/envs/disperse/bin/netconv \
  --skelconv-bin /Users/fules/miniforge3/envs/disperse/bin/skelconv \
  --output-csv outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/topology_stats.csv

You should see the [info] Converting ... lines, followed by loaded ID counts and a [done] wrote ...csv message. If any ID count shows 0, check that the unsmoothed VTU/VTP files exist (including the .S000 variant) and that true_index/cell fields are present.

Even with correct indexing, walls/filaments will generally differ from Delaunay: their vertices are generated along manifolds/skeletons and the exporter interpolates or re-samples the scalar fields onto those new vertices. Filament VTPs also don’t carry mass at all. That’s why the overlap script always pulls scalars from the Delaunay mesh only and uses IDs just for membership.

paths = {
    "delaunay": ("outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_nosmooth.vtu", "true_index"),

}

def read(path):
    r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if path.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
    r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
    return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

d = {k: read(v[0]) for k, v in paths.items()}

dl_ids = np.array(d["delaunay"].PointData[paths["delaunay"][1]], dtype=int)
wl_ids = np.array(d["walls"].PointData[paths["walls"][1]], dtype=int)
fl_ids = np.array([int(float(x)) for x in d["filaments"].PointData[paths["filaments"][1]]], dtype=int)

dl_map = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(dl_ids)}

        fv = d["filaments"].PointData[field][fi] if f_has else None
        print(f"ID {cid} {field}: delaunay={dv}, walls={wv}, filaments={fv}")

03:59:21Z — assistant

Your sample is now indexed correctly; the remaining differences come from the data itself:

  • The filament VTP stores its own scalar arrays. Even when field_value happens to match Delaunay, the filament log_field_value is in log10, while Delaunay/walls log_field_value is natural log. For example log10(0.600874…)=‑0.221 (filaments) vs ln(0.600874…)=‑0.509 (Delaunay/walls). You can verify with:

    fv = d["filaments"].PointData["field_value"]
lv = d["filaments"].PointData["log_field_value"]
import numpy as np
print(np.max(np.abs(lv - np.log10(fv))))  # should be ~0

  • In many cases the filament field_value itself differs because skeleton points are along arcs and their scalars are re-sampled/interpolated by MSE/skelconv; they’re not guaranteed to be the exact vertex values from the Delaunay mesh. Mass isn’t written to the filaments at all.

This is why ndtopo_stats.py always pulls scalars from the Delaunay mesh and only uses IDs to decide membership. If you need consistent logs, compute them yourself from the Delaunay field_value (e.g., np.log or np.log10) rather than trusting the filament log_field_value array.

04:15:25Z — user

Are we only using those filament points that have a zero decimal? Are the interpolated points differing in the decimal place?

04:15:41Z — assistant

The script doesn’t filter to “.0” entries. In the VTP converted from NDskl, the cell field is a float that encodes which Delaunay cell the skeleton point comes from; the decimal suffix (.0/.1/.2/.3) is used to distinguish the cell type (min/saddle/etc). Points sampled along arcs get the same integer part as the critical cell they’re tied to, so casting to int(cell) keeps them in the same bucket. That’s why the code uses int(float(cell)) for IDs.

Those interpolated points carry scalar values interpolated along the arc, so their field_value/log_field_value can differ from the original vertex values. For aggregation we ignore the filament scalars and take scalars from the Delaunay mesh keyed by the integer ID.

questions about the topology_stats.csv: why is the filament count so much greater than the filament mass (in all other cases the numebrs match).

05:01:14Z — assistant

The CSV mass comes from the Delaunay mesh, not from the filament file. The “filament count” is just len(filament IDs), but the “filament mass” is the sum of mass on those IDs that the script can actually match in the Delaunay point data. If some filament IDs don’t exist in the Delaunay universe (e.g., because of smoothed/interpolated skeleton points, or because the cell field doesn’t map cleanly back), they drop out of the mass sum, so mass < count.

Quick check to see how many filament IDs match the Delaunay IDs:

python - <<'PY'
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
import numpy as np

delaunay = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_nosmooth.vtu"
filaments = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U_nosmooth.S000.vtp"

def rd(path):
    r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if path.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
    r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
    return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

d = rd(delaunay)
f = rd(filaments)

uni_ids = set(np.array(d.PointData["true_index"], dtype=int))
fil_ids = np.array([int(float(x)) for x in f.PointData["cell"]], dtype=int)
fil_set = set(fil_ids)
matched = fil_set & uni_ids
print("filament IDs:", len(fil_set))
print("matched in Delaunay:", len(matched))

05:05:50Z — assistant

The integer part of cell in an unsmoothed NDskl does correspond to the source cell/critical point ID, and when you convert that NDskl to an unsmoothed VTP (-smooth 0 or *_nosmooth.vtp), those integer IDs should match the true_index in the Delaunay mesh.

When filament count ≫ filament mass in the CSV, it means some filament IDs didn’t resolve in the Delaunay universe, so their mass wasn’t added. Typical causes:

  • Using a smoothed skeleton (e.g., .S020) — spline-resampled points can carry cell values that no longer map cleanly back, or the file may drop cell altogether.
  • Using a VTP that’s been filtered/processed so cell got lost or altered.
  • Using a Delaunay file where the true_index field is missing or was renamed.

To verify, run the quick overlap check I shared (counts of filament IDs vs how many are found in Delaunay). If you see a gap, switch to unsmoothed conversions (--write-vtk → *_nosmooth.vtp/.vtu), and keep walls-id-field=true_index, filaments-id-field=cell. If the filament IDs fully match the Delaunay IDs, filament mass should align with count (assuming mass=1 per particle in the Delaunay file).

05:08:11Z — assistant

When filament mass < filament count it means many filament IDs aren’t found in the Delaunay point IDs, so their mass never gets added. With --write-vtk the converter makes _nosmooth VTP/VTU files and we take IDs from int(cell) (filaments) and true_index (Delaunay). If those sets don’t overlap fully, mass drops.

Please run this quick check to see how many filament IDs actually match the Delaunay IDs and whether there are negative/odd cell values:

python - <<'PY'
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
import numpy as np

delaunay = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_nosmooth.vtu"
filaments = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U_nosmooth.S000.vtp"

def rd(path):
    r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if path.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
    r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
    return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

d = rd(delaunay)
f = rd(filaments)

uni_ids = set(np.array(d.PointData["true_index"], dtype=int))
fil_cells = np.array(f.PointData["cell"])
fil_ids = np.array([int(float(x)) for x in fil_cells], dtype=int)
fil_set = set(fil_ids)

missing = fil_set - uni_ids
print("filament IDs total:", len(fil_set))
print("matched in Delaunay:", len(fil_set & uni_ids))
print("unmatched:", len(missing))
print("cell min/max:", fil_cells.min(), fil_cells.max())
print("negative cell count:", np.sum(fil_cells < 0))
PY
  • If unmatched is large or there are many negative cell values, those are the IDs not contributing to mass. Negative/infinity/dummy nodes from the skeleton won’t have a matching Delaunay true_index; you can filter them out before aggregation.
  • If matched still falls short even with unsmoothed VTP, double‑check that the files being read are the _nosmooth ones and that Delaunay contains the true_index array. If true_index is missing, the script will fall back to another field and IDs won’t line up.

Once we see the overlap numbers, we can decide whether to drop negative cells or adjust the ID field to get mass ≈ count.

05:10:27Z — assistant

Most of the filament points simply don’t map back to your Delaunay IDs. The quick check showed ~601k unique filament cell IDs but only ~115k of those exist in the Delaunay true_index set; the rest are unmatched. That’s why filament mass (taken from Delaunay) is far below the filament count.

Why unmatched? In the VTP, cell is a skeleton-side identifier. Only the critical-point samples line up with the original Delaunay vertex IDs; the many interpolated points along arcs carry cell values that aren’t present in the Delaunay file (note the max cell ≈ 44M vs Delaunay IDs up to ~3.3M). Those points therefore contribute to the filament count but not to mass, because there’s no Delaunay scalar to attach.

To close the gap you’d need an ID field on the filaments that truly matches the Delaunay vertices (e.g., a propagated true_index/source_index if available), or operate at the critical-point level only. With the current fields, mass can only be summed for the subset of filament points whose IDs exist in the Delaunay mesh.

06:35:04Z — assistant

That symptom usually means the slab/resample step is still using the full-domain bounds instead of the cropped tile, so when x/y shift the resample grid overlays the next tile and you see “ghost” density of the same footprint. Quick checks to confirm:

  1. Inspect the VTI bounds produced for a shifted crop:
python - <<'PY'
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLImageDataReader
r = vtkXMLImageDataReader()
r.SetFileName("outputs/quijote_batches/crop_x500000-1000000_y0-500000_z0-100000/slab_z0/crop_x500000-1000000_y0-500000_z0-100000_z0_density_3d.vti")
r.Update()
img = r.GetOutput()
print("Origin:", img.GetOrigin(), "Spacing:", img.GetSpacing(), "Extent:", img.GetExtent(), "Bounds:", img.GetBounds())
PY

If the origin/bounds still look like the global domain (e.g., starting at 0,0 instead of the crop’s x0,y0), the resampler is using full-box bounds.

  1. Likewise check the flattened density VTI and the PNG camera/center by opening the VTI in ParaView and seeing whether the bounding box matches the crop.

If you see global bounds, the fix is to have batch_clip.py resample within the clipped crop bounds rather than the original dataset. In the current script the z-origin is scaled, but x/y bounds are not re-centered per-crop before resampling, so a shifted crop samples the wrong region and the PNGs pick up neighbor tiles. Adjust the resample/clip bounds in batch_clip.py to the input data’s bounds (post-crop) before ResampleToImage/flattening; use those bounds for the render camera too.

If you want, I can patch batch_clip.py to base resampling and rendering bounds on the input dataset bounds (after cropping) so each crop stays local and the artifacts disappear.

The core issue is that we’re still telling delaunay_3D to run periodic on a box that doesn’t start at the origin. Periodic mode assumes a domain from 0 to L; when you pass a cropped NDfield with min=(500,500,100) and still use -periodic, DisPerSE wraps guard particles as if the box started at 0 and had size 1,000 Mpc/h. The NDnet log shows that: x0=[500,500,100], delta=[1000,1000,200] — it has effectively grown your 500 Mpc/h crop to a 1,000 Mpc/h periodic box, which is why you see a repeated footprint in X/Y (and Z if the delta is larger than the crop).

By contrast, the cropping logic in analyze_snapshot.py is fine: we write the NDfield header with the crop min/max, and the particle count matches the crop. It’s the periodic tessellation on a shifted box that’s causing the duplication.

To avoid the repeats for tiles that don’t start at 0:

  • Run crops with non‑periodic boundaries: --periodic false --delaunay-btype natural (or skip --periodic and set --delaunay-btype natural). This keeps the tessellation confined to the crop bounds.
  • If using batch_crop_and_clip.py, add those flags (or change defaults) so each crop is treated as a standalone non‑periodic box.

If you want to keep periodicity, you’d need to rebase coordinates so each crop starts at 0 and adjust the NDfield header accordingly, but the simpler fix is to treat cropped tiles as non‑periodic.

Cropping after Delaunay would still leave wrapped cells in the tessellation; shifting avoids introducing the extra periodic images in the first place.

how do i set up a quarto document to also produce pdf in addtion ot html

01:40:09Z — assistant

To have a Quarto doc emit both HTML and PDF:

  1. In your QMD front‑matter, list both formats:
---
title: "My Report"
format:
  html: default
  pdf:
    documentclass: article   # optional
    toc: true                # optional extras
---
  1. Ensure PDF tooling is available:
    • Install Quarto (if not already): e.g., brew install quarto.
    • Install a LaTeX engine: simplest is quarto install tinytex (or full TeX Live/MacTeX).
  2. Render both at once:
    • quarto render myfile.qmd # will produce HTML and PDF because both are listed.
    • Or, explicitly: quarto render myfile.qmd --to html,pdf.

If LaTeX is missing, PDF will fail—install tinytex via Quarto and rerun.

That file has no arc tag (U) in the name, so you see …_s5.ckup.NDskl alongside the expected manifolds file. 07:20:28Z — assistant

Understood—you want the root cause, not just an alias. A few likely reasons MSE emitted only the “backup” skeleton instead of the tagged U file, plus what to check:

  1. Persistence/cancellation can delete the requested arcs
    • If -nsig 5 is very aggressive, the simplification pass can cancel all arcs of a given tag, so no U skeleton is written and only the MSC backup remains.
    • Check the MSE log for “Cancelling pairs …” and how many arcs remain. If zero U arcs survive, there’s nothing to write.
  2. Output tag not actually requested
    • Ensure -dumpArcs U was present in the command for those crops. If a run was restarted without U, only the manifolds and backup MSC would exist.
  3. Reused prefix colliding with older outputs
    • If a previous run with the same prefix produced a backup but no U, and a later run failed/was killed before writing U, the “newest” file could be the old backup. Clean the crop folder and rerun to be sure you’re seeing a fresh MSE output.
  4. Disk/kill during write
    • A killed MSE (e.g., OOM, SIGKILL) might leave only intermediate/backup files. In your logs, verify MSE completed the skeleton dump (“Saving 3D skeleton to file … done.”).

How to investigate and resolve: - For an affected crop, rerun just MSE manually with verbose logs: mse <crop_prefix>.NDnet -outName <prefix> -outDir <dir> -nsig 5 -dumpArcs U -dumpManifolds JE1a Check the console: look for “Dumping skeleton … done.” and count of arcs. - Lower persistence temporarily (e.g., -nsig 3 or add -cut thresholds) to see if U is emitted; if so, the -nsig 5 setting is pruning everything. - Ensure the crop directory is empty before rerunning, so stale backups aren’t picked up. - Confirm the batch command actually includes --dump-arcs U for all tiles. - If MSE logs show arcs are present but the U file isn’t written, capture that log snippet; it could be a DisPerSE bug in that build.

Once you confirm arcs are being produced and written, the U file should reappear and downstream steps can use it without relying on aliases.

07:54:53Z — assistant

mse writes two skeletons: the final one for the arc tag you requested (e.g. _s5.U.NDskl) and a backup of the unsimplified complex before cancellations. That backup uses an internal tag, and in your build it shows up as _s5.C.backup.NDskl (earlier runs showed _s5.MSC.backup.NDskl). The “C” is DisPerSE’s own label for that pre-simplification/complete skeleton, not something the scripts are adding. When no _s5.U.NDskl is present but a _s5.C.backup.NDskl is, it usually means:

  • All U arcs were cancelled by the chosen persistence (-nsig 5) so no tagged skeleton was emitted, leaving only the backup, or
  • The run was interrupted or reused a directory with stale backup files and never wrote a fresh _s5.U.NDskl.

How to get the proper _s5.U.NDskl: 1) Rerun mse for that crop in a clean (or emptied) crop folder with -dumpArcs U -nsig 5 and watch the log: you should see arc counts and “Saving 3D skeleton to file …U.NDskl … done.” If the log shows zero U arcs remaining, lower -nsig or adjust cuts so arcs survive. 2) Ensure every batch call includes --dump-arcs U. 3) Avoid reusing old crop directories when debugging—old backups can be picked up as “newest” if a run fails before writing U.

Once mse actually produces _s5.U.NDskl, downstream steps will prefer that file and ignore the backup.

Unlikely it’s a filename-length issue. APFS/HFS allow ~255‑byte filenames and ~1K paths; your example name is ~80 chars, well under the limits. DisPerSE chooses the stem: when it writes the “backup” skeleton (unsimplified complex), it uses its own tag in the name—older runs showed _MSC.backup, your build is emitting _C.backup. That tag comes from MSE, not from truncation.

If you want to be sure, check the MSE log for that crop: it will print the exact “Saving 3D skeleton to file …” line. If it only prints the backup and not _s5.U.NDskl, the issue is that the tagged skeleton wasn’t written (e.g., arcs pruned/cancelled or the run interrupted), not that the name got mangled by length.

08:12:58Z — assistant

Those filenames come straight from MSE; our scripts don’t rewrite them. MSE builds its output name as:

<outName>_s<sigma>.<tag>.NDskl
  • For sigma it prints a float, so -nsig 5 becomes s5.00000.
  • <outName> is whatever prefix we pass (your long crop name ending in _z900000-1000000), so that substring naturally appears in every file.
  • The extra _z900000-1000000 you see after s5.00000 is not a truncation artifact; it’s still part of the original prefix being repeated in the composed name. MSE isn’t changing it because of length—it’s just concatenating prefix + sigma tag + “backup”.

Why no _U.NDskl then? - If MSE cancels all U arcs at nsig=5, it won’t write a tagged U skeleton and you’ll only see the backup. The MSE log will show arc counts and whether it wrote “Saving 3D skeleton to file …U.NDskl”. - If a run was interrupted or a directory reused, you can end up with only the backup file from a prior run.

How to verify/fix on a crop: 1) Clean that crop folder (or move files aside) and rerun just MSE with a shorter --output-prefix as a test: mse <crop>.NDnet -outName test -outDir <crop_dir> -nsig 5 -dumpArcs U -dumpManifolds JE1a Watch the console for “Saving 3D skeleton to file …U.NDskl” and the arc counts. 2) If the log shows zero U arcs at nsig=5, lower -nsig or adjust -cut until arcs survive, then rerun. 3) If the log shows arcs and “Saving …U.NDskl” but the file is missing, let me know—that would indicate an MSE bug rather than naming/length.

So the odd-looking _s5.00000_…backup name is MSE’s normal composition (prefix + sigma tag + “backup”), not a path-length distortion; the real issue is that a U skeleton wasn’t written for that run.

08:40:45Z — assistant

I cleaned up the naming to avoid double S000 on filament VTPs:

  • ndtopo_stats.py now strips any existing smoothing tag and, for skelconv, does not pre-append _S000—since skelconv adds .S000 itself when -smooth 0 is used. It looks for foo.vtp, foo_S000.vtp, or foo.S000.vtp after conversion.
  • Netconv unsmoothed VTU still uses a single _S000 suffix.

Re-run the batch; the filament VTP should come out with only one S000 and the stats step won’t fail on a missing file.

08:53:08Z — user

does the ndtopo_stat.py script test for the existinece of S000 files before it generates them?

08:53:16Z — assistant

Yes. In ndtopo_stats.py, both converters check for an existing unsmoothed file before running netconv/skelconv:

  • For NDnet → VTU: it strips any existing smoothing tag and looks for <stem>_S000.vtu. If found, it uses it; otherwise it runs netconv … -smooth 0 to create it.
  • For NDskl → VTP: it strips any smoothing tag and looks for foo.vtp, foo_S000.vtp, or foo.S000.vtp. If any exist, it uses the existing one; only if none are present does it call skelconv … -smooth 0 to generate it.

So it will reuse existing _S000 outputs and only generate them when missing.

17:33:27Z — assistant

The key failure is Error code "No space left on device" from the VTK writers—that corrupted the partially written VTK/PNG files, leading to downstream read errors (offsets array is not long enough, File not readable). This wasn’t caused by the code logic; it’s a disk/full-quota issue.

How to recover: 1) Free space (disk/quota) where outputs/ lives. Check df -h or your quota. 2) Delete the incomplete slab folder so it can be regenerated cleanly: rm -rf outputs/quijote_batches/crop_x0-500_y500-1000_z700-800/slab_z700 3) Re-run just that slab (or rerun the batch for that crop once space is available).

After space is freed, the “offsets not long enough” and PNG write errors will disappear because the writers will complete successfully. If you want, I can add a guard to skip PNGs/reads when a write fails, but the root cause here is insufficient disk space.

To fix the positioning: - Use the shifted density VTK from analyze_snapshot.py (e.g., ..._delaunay.vtu or the smoothed version) as --delaunay in batch_clip.py, not the _S000 rebased file; or - If you truly need the unsmoothed version, convert with the crop shift applied (not currently available in the auto-conversion).

can you explain what the batch_corp_and_clip.py script does in lines 205-230. I suspect that somethign there leads to a wrong flie being grabbed.

21:24:54Z — assistant

Between lines ~205–230 of scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py, the script resolves which VTKs to feed into batch_clip.py for each crop:

  • It builds smoothing suffixes from --netconv-smooth/--skelconv-smooth/--delaunay-smooth, e.g., .S020.
  • It then searches the crop folder for the latest matching files:
    • Manifolds: crop_*manifolds_<dump_manifolds>*<manifolds_suffix>.vtu (fallback: any manifolds_<dump_manifolds>.vtu).
    • Filaments: crop_*<dump_arcs>*<filaments_suffix>.vtp (fallback: any <dump_arcs>.vtp).
    • Delaunay: crop_*delaunay*<delaunay_suffix>.vtu (fallback: any delaunay*.vtu).
  • If none are found, it prints a warning and skips slabs for that crop.
  • The chosen files are passed to batch_clip.py for slab clipping, flattening, resampling, PNG rendering, etc.

If the wrong file is being grabbed, it’s typically because multiple variants exist (e.g., a rebased _S000 from ndtopo_stats.py --write-vtk and a shifted ..._delaunay.vtu). The glob picks the lexicographically latest match. To avoid pulling the unsmoothed, unshifted _S000 file, make sure the only matching files in the crop directory are the globally shifted exports from analyze_snapshot.py (e.g., ..._delaunay.vtu, ..._manifolds_*.S020.vtu, ..._arcs_*.S020.vtp) or adjust the glob to prefer non-S000 files.

08:11:06Z — user

there are two ways to analyze filaments in disperse. 1) via arcs, 2) via manifolds with the 2a setting. what is the difference between these methods?

08:11:27Z — assistant

In DisPerSE, 1-saddles are the critical points associated with filaments, and there are two ways to extract their geometry:

  1. Arcs (-dumpArcs U or similar)
    • You get the 1D skeleton: polyline segments connecting critical points (minima ↔︎ 1-saddles ↔︎ maxima, depending on the arc type).
    • Output: NDskl (and VTP after skelconv).
    • Pros: clean, thin “spines” of filaments; easy to overlay; lightweight.
    • Cons: 1D only—no filament cross-section or surface extent.
  2. Manifolds with 2a (-dumpManifolds J…2a or similar)
    • You extract descending 2-manifolds from 1-saddles (the “walls” of filaments), giving a 2D surface representation of filament cross-sections.
    • Output: NDnet (and VTU after netconv).
    • Pros: captures filament thickness/cross-section; can be used to measure area/volume around filaments.
    • Cons: heavier geometry; surfaces can be more sensitive to smoothing/persistence choices.

So arcs give you the filament spine (1D skeleton), while 2a manifolds give you the filament surfaces emanating from 1-saddles. You choose based on whether you need just the spine (arcs) or a surface representation (2a manifolds).

08:14:57Z — user

Which option should i choose if i am trying to determine the proportion of particles associated with filaments and walls?

08:15:05Z — assistant

Use the skeleton/arcs for filaments and the standard wall manifolds:

  • Walls: use the descending manifolds (e.g., JE1a) from -dumpManifolds to identify wall membership.
  • Filaments: use the 1D skeleton (-dumpArcs U) to identify filament membership.

Then map those IDs back to the Delaunay vertices (or snapshot particles) to count how many are in walls, filaments, both, or neither. The 2a manifolds give you filament surfaces/thickness but don’t add clarity for counting particle/vertex association; the arcs are the canonical filament identity for overlap/association tasks.

08:18:43Z — user

What do you mean by filament surface/thickness? How should i imagine/picture/visualize that?

08:18:49Z — assistant

Think of a filament as a tube. The arc is the thin curve running along the tube’s centerline (the spine). The 2a manifold is the 2D surface that wraps around that spine—like the skin of the tube—capturing where the field descends toward the 1-saddle along two dimensions. Visualizing 2a manifolds shows you the filament’s cross-sectional footprint and how far it extends off the spine; visualizing arcs shows only the central line.

  • Data acquisition → analyze_snapshot.py (stream/crop/stride → Delaunay → MSE) → shifted VTK exports.

#### 16:45:46Z — assistant

Here’s a simple `pvpython` script to load a 3D VTU/VTP, rotate/zoom the camera, and write an MP4. `pvpython` is appropriate for this (headless ParaView); alternatives are PyVista (VTK + off-screen via OSMesa/EGL) or raw VTK with an image writer loop.

Save as `scripts/spin_render.py`:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env pvpython
import argparse
from paraview.simple import *

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--input", required=True, help="VTU/VTP/PLY/etc.")
    ap.add_argument("--output", required=True, help="Output MP4 (e.g., spin.mp4)")
    ap.add_argument("--frames", type=int, default=180, help="Number of frames in the spin")
    ap.add_argument("--elev", type=float, default=20.0, help="Camera elevation in degrees")
    ap.add_argument("--zoom", type=float, default=1.2, help="Zoom factor")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    src = OpenDataFile(args.input)
    view = CreateRenderView()
    view.ViewSize = [1280, 720]
    view.Background = [1, 1, 1]

    disp = Show(src, view)
    disp.Representation = "Surface"
    disp.SetScalarBarVisibility(view, False)
    ColorBy(disp, None)
    view.ResetCamera()
    # apply elevation and zoom
    cam = view.GetActiveCamera()
    cam.Elevation(args.elev)
    view.Camera.Zoom(args.zoom)

    # set up animation
    anim = GetAnimationScene()
    anim.EndTime = args.frames
    cam_anim = GetCameraTrack(view)
    cam_anim.Mode = 'Path'
    cam_anim.ShowCameraPath = 0
    cam_anim.Points = []
    for i in range(args.frames + 1):
        t = float(i)
        angle = 360.0 * i / args.frames
        cam.Elevation(0)  # keep elevation fixed
        cam.Azimuth(angle)  # rotate
        cam_anim.Points.append([t, cam.GetPosition()[0], cam.GetPosition()[1], cam.GetPosition()[2],
                                cam.GetFocalPoint()[0], cam.GetFocalPoint()[1], cam.GetFocalPoint()[2],
                                cam.GetViewUp()[0], cam.GetViewUp()[1], cam.GetViewUp()[2]])
    anim.PlayMode = 'Sequence'
    anim.NumberOfFrames = args.frames

    WriteAnimation(args.output, view=view, FrameRate=30, Compression=True)
    Delete(view); Delete(src)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run:

  --output outputs/quijote_batches/crop_x500-1000_y500-1000_z0-100/spin.mp4 \
  --frames 180 --elev 20 --zoom 1.2

Options: - pvpython (shown) for ParaView’s off-screen rendering and animation export. - PyVista (pip install pyvista imageio) for a pure-Python/VTK workflow; use plotter.open_movie, rotate the camera, and write frames. - Raw VTK (vtkRenderer/vtkRenderWindow/vtkWindowToImageFilter/vtkPNGWriter) with a loop over camera azimuth/elevation and ffmpeg to stitch frames.

17:17:51Z — assistant

It colors by the first point-data array in the file. If the dataset has no point arrays, it falls back to a solid light gray.

So in your case it’s whichever array is stored first in that VTU (often field_value or log_field_value, but it depends on the file’s array order).

18:04:27Z — user

what are the possible ranges for elev, and zoom?

18:04:34Z — assistant

  • --elev is in degrees. Technically any real value works; typical useful range is about -90 to +90 (negative tilts downward, positive upward). Values beyond that just flip the view and can look odd.
  • --zoom is a multiplicative factor.
    • > 1 zooms in (e.g., 1.2, 2.0)
    • < 1 zooms out (e.g., 0.8, 0.5)
    • Must be positive; 1.0 means no change.

I need to change the git credentials on this laptop and then modify all past commits in this repository so that they are reflecting the new credentials both locally and on github. how can i proceed?

07:43:40Z — assistant

Short version: you need to (1) update your local Git identity/credentials, (2) rewrite commit history to replace old author/committer info, then (3) force‑push to GitHub. This is a history rewrite (disruptive for collaborators and tags/PRs), so make sure you really want it.

Here’s a safe, explicit path:

1) Update your local Git identity (new author info for future commits)

git config --global user.name "New Name"
git config --global user.email "new@email.com"

If this repo should use a different identity:

git config user.name "New Name"
git config user.email "new@email.com"

2) Update GitHub authentication (for pushing) If you use HTTPS with a token:

git remote -v

Generate a new GitHub PAT if needed, then update stored credentials in your OS keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, etc.) or switch to SSH.

3) Rewrite all commit author/committer metadata Recommended tool: git filter-repo (faster/safer than old filter-branch).

Install if needed:

brew install git-filter-repo
##### or: pip install git-filter-repo

Then rewrite:

git filter-repo --force --mailmap <(cat <<'EOF'
Old Name <old@email.com> New Name <new@email.com>
EOF
)

If you have multiple old emails, add more lines in the mailmap.

4) Force-push rewritten history

git push --force --all
git push --force --tags

Important caveats - This rewrites commit hashes. Any collaborators must re-clone or hard reset. - PRs referencing old SHAs will break. - GitHub caches may still show old info in places until it reindexes.

If you want, I can tailor the exact commands to your repo (e.g., multiple old emails, or only rewriting this repo not global), but I’d need: - old name/email(s) - new name/email - whether you want to rewrite all branches/tags or only main

Below is a one‑off merge you can run in the terminal (no script changes):

python - <<'PY'
import glob, h5py, numpy as np, os

parts = sorted(glob.glob("snapdir_000/snap_000.*.hdf5"))
out = "snapdir_000/snap_000_merged.hdf5"

assert parts, "No snapshot parts found"

with h5py.File(parts[0], "r") as f0, h5py.File(out, "w") as fout:
    # Copy non-particle groups from first file
    for key in f0.keys():
        if key == "PartType1":
            continue
        fout.copy(f0[key], key)

    # Merge PartType1 datasets across all parts
    fout.create_group("PartType1")
    datasets = list(f0["PartType1"].keys())

    # Compute total particles
    total = 0
    for p in parts:
        with h5py.File(p, "r") as f:
            total += f["PartType1"][datasets[0]].shape[0]

    # Create output datasets
    for dname in datasets:
        d0 = f0["PartType1"][dname]
        shape = (total,) + d0.shape[1:]
        fout["PartType1"].create_dataset(dname, shape=shape, dtype=d0.dtype)

    # Write in chunks
    offset = 0
    for p in parts:
        with h5py.File(p, "r") as f:
            n = f["PartType1"][datasets[0]].shape[0]
            for dname in datasets:
                fout["PartType1"][dname][offset:offset+n] = f["PartType1"][dname][:]
            offset += n

    # Update Header
    hdr = fout["Header"].attrs
    hdr["NumPart_ThisFile"] = np.array([0, total, 0, 0, 0, 0], dtype=hdr["NumPart_ThisFile"].dtype)
    hdr["NumPart_Total"] = np.array([0, total, 0, 0, 0, 0], dtype=hdr["NumPart_Total"].dtype)
    hdr["NumFilesPerSnapshot"] = 1
    if "NumPart_Total_HighWord" in hdr:
        hdr["NumPart_Total_HighWord"] = np.zeros(6, dtype=hdr["NumPart_Total_HighWord"].dtype)

print("Wrote:", out)
PY

If you want no script changes, you cannot just point analyze_snapshot.py at a folder. That script uses plain h5py and expects a single HDF5 file, so it won’t automatically traverse snap_000.0.hdf5 … snap_000.9.hdf5.

The clean way to get “multi‑file behavior” without copying the data is to create a Virtual Dataset (VDS) file that references all 10 parts. This produces one tiny HDF5 file that behaves like a single merged snapshot, while still reading from the original parts on disk.

Do this once per snapshot directory
python - <<'PY'
import glob, h5py, numpy as np

parts = sorted(glob.glob("snapdir_000/snap_000.*.hdf5"))
out = "snapdir_000/snap_000_vds.hdf5"

assert parts, "No snapshot parts found."

with h5py.File(parts[0], "r") as f0, h5py.File(out, "w", libver="latest") as fout:
    # copy non-particle groups
    for key in f0.keys():
        if key.startswith("PartType"):
            continue
        fout.copy(f0[key], key)

    part_groups = [k for k in f0.keys() if k.startswith("PartType")]
    totals = {g: 0 for g in part_groups}
    datasets = {g: list(f0[g].keys()) for g in part_groups}

    # count totals
    for p in parts:
        with h5py.File(p, "r") as f:
            for g in part_groups:
                totals[g] += f[g][datasets[g][0]].shape[0]

    # build VDS for each PartType dataset
    for g in part_groups:
        g_out = fout.create_group(g)
        for dname in datasets[g]:
            d0 = f0[g][dname]
            shape = (totals[g],) + d0.shape[1:]
            layout = h5py.VirtualLayout(shape=shape, dtype=d0.dtype)

            offset = 0
            for p in parts:
                with h5py.File(p, "r") as f:
                    src = h5py.VirtualSource(f[g][dname])
                    n = f[g][dname].shape[0]
                    layout[offset:offset+n] = src
                    offset += n

            g_out.create_virtual_dataset(dname, layout, fillvalue=0)

    # update Header counts
    hdr = fout["Header"].attrs
    counts = np.zeros(6, dtype=hdr["NumPart_Total"].dtype)
    for g, n in totals.items():
        idx = int(g.replace("PartType", ""))
        counts[idx] = n
    hdr["NumPart_ThisFile"] = counts
    hdr["NumPart_Total"] = counts
    hdr["NumFilesPerSnapshot"] = 1
    if "NumPart_Total_HighWord" in hdr:
        hdr["NumPart_Total_HighWord"] = np.zeros(6, dtype=hdr["NumPart_Total_HighWord"].dtype)

print("Wrote:", out)
PY
Then run your pipeline as usual
python scripts/analyze_snapshot.py --input snapdir_000/snap_000_vds.hdf5 ...

Important: the VDS file only references the original parts. If you move/delete the part files, the VDS won’t work.

07:03:22Z — user

how is the coloring of log field value determined?

07:03:40Z — assistant

It’s a straightforward scalar‑to‑color mapping:

  • The script uses the log_field_value array directly (no additional log transform).
  • It applies a ParaView colormap preset (currently default Fast).
  • Then it maps values to colors linearly across a range:
    • Auto‑range: min/max come from the data.
    • Fixed range: you set --range-min/--range-max; values outside clamp to the end colors.

So the “coloring” is entirely determined by: 1) which array is used (log_field_value), 2) which colormap preset (e.g., Fast), 3) which range (auto or fixed).

If you want a different mapping (e.g., log scale, different preset), that’s a separate setting.

07:17:40Z — user

Based on the figures there are only very few values near max and therefore the coloring seems compressed to the low range. It would be useful to add more color separation at the low range. How can it be done?

07:18:32Z — assistant

You’re seeing that because a few high outliers stretch the range, so most values map into a tiny part of the colormap. The standard fix is to clip the range (e.g., use percentiles) so low values get more color separation.

Recommended approach: percentile clipping
  1. Compute a low/high percentile from the data.
/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/bin/pvpython - <<'PY'
from paraview.simple import OpenDataFile
from paraview import servermanager as sm
from vtkmodules.util.numpy_support import vtk_to_numpy
import numpy as np

src = OpenDataFile("outputs/quijote_batches/crop_x500-1000_y500-1000_z0-100/crop_x500-1000_y500-1000_z0-100_s5_manifolds_JE1a_S020.vtu")
src.UpdatePipeline()
data = sm.Fetch(src)
arr = vtk_to_numpy(data.GetPointData().GetArray("log_field_value"))
print("p1,p99:", np.quantile(arr, [0.01, 0.99]))
PY
  1. Use that range in spin_render.py:
--range-min=<p1> --range-max=<p99>
Alternative: manual clipping

Just pick a tighter range (e.g., --range-min -3 --range-max 3) until the contrast looks good.

Why I’m not suggesting log scale

You’re already plotting log_field_value, so an additional log scale usually isn’t appropriate (and it won’t work if values are negative).

If you want, I can add a --percentile-range 1 99 option to compute this automatically.

16:58:18Z — assistant

Those warnings are coming from NumPy reductions (sum/mean) on very large arrays during the summary‑stats step in batch_clip.py. The arrays coming from ParaView are often float32, and summing millions of values (especially mass/density fields with large magnitudes) can overflow that dtype, so NumPy emits:

RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in reduce

Key points: - It happens after the files are written, during the stats calculation. - It does not affect the written VTU/VTP/VTI outputs—only the summary stats (sum/mean) may be unreliable for those arrays.

If you want to eliminate the warnings or improve the stats accuracy, I can: 1) compute stats in float64, or
2) skip stats for specific arrays, or
3) add a --skip-stats flag.

Tell me which you prefer.

19:07:30Z — user

How does this warning affect the stats calculation. What is the impact on the stats?

19:07:45Z — assistant

Impact of the warning:

  • It means the intermediate sum (and mean) overflowed the numeric type during the reduction.
  • When that happens:
    • sum is wrong (often becomes inf or wraps).
    • mean is wrong (because it’s derived from that sum).
    • std can also be wrong (it depends on sums of squares).
  • min, max, and quantiles (q25/median/q75) are not affected, because they don’t rely on summing.

So the stats CSV rows for those arrays should be treated like this:

  • Reliable: min, max, q25, median, q75, count
  • Potentially wrong when warning appears: sum, mean, std

If you want, I can make the stats step cast to float64 to avoid overflow and keep all stats accurate.

19:10:24Z — user

accuracty of stats is important so yes please fix the code to make them accurate. both for the slabs and the crop/clip.

19:12:01Z — assistant

I fixed the stats overflow in all three places that generate CSVs:

  • scripts/batch_clip.py (slab stats)
  • scripts/analyze_snapshot.py (crop summary stats)
  • scripts/ndtopo_stats.py (topology stats)

All now compute sums/means/std in float64, which avoids the overflow warnings and keeps stats accurate.

To get clean stats, rerun the step(s) that generate the CSVs: - For slab stats: rerun batch_clip.py (or batch_crop_and_clip.py). - For crop summary stats: rerun analyze_snapshot.py. - For topology stats: rerun ndtopo_stats.py or the batch driver.

If you want, I can also add a small note to the docs about the stats now being computed in float64.

22:37:36Z — assistant

I see two different “warnings” in your log, and they’re not the same thing:

  1. The “Only X/Y points are unique” warning is from delaunay_3D itself. That’s normal when there are duplicate coordinates (boundary/guard particles). It doesn’t come from our stats code and won’t be removed by the scaling changes.

  2. The crash you hit (NoneType on GetPoints().GetData()) is new and is in our code path. That happens when a slab clip yields zero points, so VTK returns no points object.

I fixed the crash by making average_unstructured_to_2d() write a zero-filled VTI whenever the clip is empty (or the scalar array is missing), instead of raising. I also tightened the histogram averaging to scale values before binning to avoid overflow in that path.

Changes: - scripts/batch_clip.py
- average_unstructured_to_2d() now: - handles empty clips gracefully (writes zeros instead of crashing) - scales values before histogram binning to avoid overflow - filters non‑finite values

Please re-run the same command after pulling the latest changes. You should see: - No crash on empty slabs. - No numpy overflow warnings from the slab averaging path. - The “Only X/Y points are unique” warning will still appear (that’s from DisPerSE).

If you still see RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in reduce, paste just that warning block and I’ll trace the remaining source (it would then be coming from a different code path than the ones we updated).

If you want, I can also add a short [warn] line when a slab is empty so it’s obvious why the average VTI is blank.

23:45:07Z — user

but why did the crash just shoe up now? did any of the recent code changes cause it?

23:45:42Z — assistant

Short answer: the crash was always possible; you just hit the empty‑slab path for the first time.

What happened: - average_unstructured_to_2d() calls servermanager.Fetch() on the clipped dataset and then expects points. - If the slab is outside the data bounds (or contains zero points), GetPoints() is None, so GetPoints().GetData() crashes. - That can happen when you pass a global slab origin (e.g., z=900) but the VTK you’re clipping is still in rebased/local coordinates (0–100). Then the slab is empty.

Why now: - Recent changes made the workflow actually find/use the correct files (instead of skipping slabs or picking a different file), so the empty‑slab path is now being exercised.

I’ve already patched this to handle empty slabs gracefully (write zero‑filled VTI + warn instead of crashing). If you want to avoid empty slabs altogether, we should make sure the VTKs are shifted back to global coords or pass slab origins in the crop’s local frame.

If you want, I can add a debug print showing the file bounds vs. slab range so it’s obvious when a slab is out of bounds.

Short answer: No — the integer‐cell logic is only meaningful for skeletons, not for walls.

Why walls match now
- In *_topology_stats.csv, walls are matched by true_index back to the Delaunay NDnet.
- The walls NDnet is a sub‑network of the Delaunay vertices, so true_index is the right key.
- That’s why wall stats in *_summary_stats.csv and *_topology_stats.csv line up.

Why filaments diverge
- Filaments come from NDskl/VTK skeletons, where cell is not a vertex ID for all points.
- The decimal part of cell encodes the simplex dimension (0‑cell, 1‑cell, 2‑cell, etc.).
- Taking int(cell) collapses all those and incorrectly maps many interpolated filament points onto Delaunay vertex IDs.
- So topology stats (Delaunay‑based) and summary stats (filament‑based) diverge — especially for filaments.

Would integer cell logic apply to walls?
No. In NDnet (walls), the cell array is not the same semantic as in NDskl. For walls, true_index is the correct mapping and should stay.

If you want better filament consistency, the right fix is: - only map 0‑cells (where cell has .0) back to Delaunay, and ignore interpolated points.
This would make filament topology stats “Delaunay‑consistent,” but it will not match filament summary stats (which include interpolated points).

If you want, I can implement a flag like: - --filaments-cell-mode zero (only .0 cells) - --filaments-cell-mode all (current behavior)

    • count_unmatched (diagnostic)

Yes—at the summary level the labels aren’t exclusive by design. walls, filaments, and filament_manifolds are overlapping sets, with separate “shared_*” rows to show overlaps.

For the new per‑point CSV, I made categories exclusive by applying a priority order in classify_id (so each Delaunay ID gets a single label). That means the per‑point file is exclusive, even though the summary categories are not.

If you want the per‑point file to keep multi‑membership, I can change it to either: 1) add boolean columns (is_wall, is_filament, is_filament_manifold, plus shared flags), or
2) keep a category_list column with all labels a point belongs to.

Which do you prefer?

07:04:56Z — user

I think the boolean column options is easier to handle in subsequent analysis.

07:05:27Z — assistant

Done. The per‑point CSV now includes boolean membership flags while keeping the exclusive category label.

Changes - scripts/ndtopo_stats.py: per‑point output now writes is_wall, is_filament, is_filament_manifold (0/1) for each Delaunay ID. - docs/ND_TOPO_STATS_USER_GUIDE.qmd: updated the per‑point CSV description.

If you want additional boolean columns (e.g., is_shared_wall_filament, is_shared_wall_filament_manifold, etc.) let me know and I’ll add them.

If you want additional boolean flags (e.g., is_shared_wall_filament, is_shared_wall_filament_manifold), I can add those too.

Added a pass‑through flag in scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py:

  • When set, it writes <crop_prefix>_topology_points.csv per crop and passes --per-point-csv to ndtopo_stats.py.

07:14:56Z — user

can you give me a prompt for batch crop and clip with this option (or if it is default, i don’t need to modify?)

07:15:05Z — assistant

It’s opt‑in, not default. Add --write-per-point-csv to your usual command, e.g.:

python scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py \
  --snapshot data/snapdir_000 \
  --output-root outputs/quijote_batches_000 \
  --crop-size 500000 500000 100000 \
  --mse-nsig 3.5 \
  --x-range 500000 1000000 --y-range 500000 1000000 --z-range 900000 1000000 \
  --slab-step 10 --slab-thickness 10 \
  --dump-manifolds JE1a --dump-arcs U \
  --netconv-smooth 20 --skelconv-smooth 20 \
  --png-percentile-range 0 99 \
  --write-per-point-csv

This will add <crop_prefix>_topology_points.csv in each crop folder.

07:16:53Z — user

how woudl i run batch crop and clip if i don’t need the slabs? does it mean no clip?

07:17:05Z — assistant

batch_crop_and_clip.py always runs slabs; there isn’t a “no‑clip” flag right now. If you don’t want slabs:

  1. Run only analyze_snapshot.py (either manually or via a small loop), and skip batch_clip.py entirely.
  2. If you want to keep using batch_crop_and_clip.py, I can add a --skip-slabs flag that bypasses the clipping step.

Setting a huge --slab-step won’t fully skip slabs, because it still runs the first one. If you want the flag, I can add it.

07:18:31Z — user

sorry, don’t understand what you mean huge –slab-step.

07:18:39Z — assistant

I meant: even if you set --slab-step very large, the script will still run one slab (the first origin in each crop), so it’s not a true “no‑clip” mode. There isn’t a way to disable slabs without changing the script.

If you want “no slabs,” your options are: 1) Run only analyze_snapshot.py (no batch clip at all), or
2) I can add a --skip-slabs flag to batch_crop_and_clip.py so it only does the analyze step and topology stats.

Tell me which you prefer.
