07:33:30Z — assistant

It didn’t run because your command line dropped the flag: there’s no trailing \ after --png-percentile-range 0 95, so --write-per-point-csv was treated as a separate shell command and ignored.

Use this (note the backslash):

python scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py \
  --snapshot data/snapdir_000 \
  --output-root outputs/quijote_batches_000_test_2fil \
  --crop-size 500000 500000 100000 \
  --mse-nsig 3.5 \
  --x-range 500000 1000000 --y-range 500000 1000000 --z-range 900000 1000000 \
  --slab-step 10 --slab-thickness 10 \
  --dump-manifolds JE1a --dump-arcs U \
  --dump-filament-manifolds JE2a \
  --netconv-smooth 20 --skelconv-smooth 20 \
  --png-percentile-range 0 95 \
  --write-per-point-csv

That will create <crop_prefix>_topology_points.csv in each crop folder.

08:04:54Z — user

Can you add a –skip-slabs flag to batch_crop_and_clip.py so it skips the slabs.

08:05:19Z — assistant

Added --skip-slabs to scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py and documented it in docs/BATCH_CROP_AND_CLIP_USER_GUIDE.qmd.

Usage example:

python scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py \
  --snapshot data/snapdir_000 \
  --output-root outputs/quijote_batches_000 \
  --crop-size 500000 500000 100000 \
  --mse-nsig 3.5 \
  --x-range 500000 1000000 --y-range 500000 1000000 --z-range 900000 1000000 \
  --dump-manifolds JE1a --dump-arcs U \
  --skip-slabs

This will run only analyze_snapshot.py + topology stats per crop, skipping batch_clip.py slabs entirely.

17:23:18Z — user

can you generate a script that pulls together all topology_points.csv files from all crops and generates from the total the same statistics as in the topology_stats.csv file. In addition, generate histograms for each of those categories.

17:25:24Z — assistant

I added scripts/aggregate_topology_points.py. It scans all *_topology_points.csv files, computes combined topology_stats (same columns as the per‑crop stats), and writes histograms per category & scalar (CSV always, PNG if matplotlib is available).

Yes—there are two common “combine” meanings. Which one do you want?

A) Concatenate all MP4s into one long movie (back‑to‑back).
From the movies folder:

cd outputs/quijote_batches_000_slabs/movies
printf "file '%s'\n" "$PWD"/*.mp4 > concat.txt
ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i concat.txt -c copy combined.mp4

If -c copy fails (different sizes/codecs), re‑encode:

ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i concat.txt -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p combined.mp4

B) Tile multiple movies into a grid (side‑by‑side).
Example for 2 videos:

ffmpeg -i a.mp4 -i b.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]hstack=inputs=2[v]" -map "[v]" tiled.mp4

(For 2×2 or more, use xstack; I can generate that once you tell me how many tiles.)

If you instead want to combine all PNGs directly, that usually means first converting each sequence to MP4 (what the stitch script already does) and then concatenating the MP4s as in A. 08:20:41Z — user

a single pngs sequence across crops and order by z

08:21:08Z — assistant

Yes. Here’s a one‑shot command that builds a single PNG sequence across all crops, ordered by slab z (with crop name as a tie‑breaker), then encodes to MP4. Adjust suffix to the PNG type you want.

python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import re, subprocess, shutil, sys

root = Path("outputs/quijote_batches_000_slabs")
suffix = "walls_3d.png"  # <-- change this
fps = 30

frames = []
for crop in sorted(root.glob("crop_*")):
    for slab in crop.glob("slab_z*"):
        m = re.search(r"slab_z(-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)", slab.name)
        if not m:
            continue
        z = float(m.group(1))
        matches = sorted(slab.glob(f"*_{suffix}"))
        if matches:
            frames.append((z, crop.name, matches[0].resolve()))

frames.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))  # order by z, then crop name

out_dir = root / "movies"
out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
list_path = out_dir / f"all_{suffix.replace('.', '_')}.ffmpeg.txt"
with open(list_path, "w") as f:
    for _, _, p in frames:
        f.write(f"file '{p.as_posix()}'\n")

ffmpeg = shutil.which("ffmpeg")
if not ffmpeg:
    sys.exit("ffmpeg not found on PATH")

out_mp4 = out_dir / f"all_{suffix.replace('.', '_')}.mp4"
subprocess.run(
    [ffmpeg, "-y", "-f", "concat", "-safe", "0", "-i", str(list_path),
     "-r", str(fps), "-c:v", "libx264", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", str(out_mp4)],
    check=True,
)
print("wrote", out_mp4)
PY

08:25:26Z — assistant

ffmpeg is refusing to overwrite because we run it with -n unless you pass --overwrite. Just re-run with that flag:

python scripts/stitch_slab_pngs.py \
  --root outputs/quijote_batches_000_slabs \
  --png-suffix walls_3d.png \
  --combine-all \
  --output-dir outputs/quijote_batches_000_slabs/movies \
  --frame-hold 3 \
  --fps 15 \
  --overwrite

That will replace the existing all_walls_3d_png.mp4.

08:28:18Z — assistant

The fast playback is from ffmpeg dropping frames (see the DTS/PTS “invalid dropping” lines). That happens because the concat list has no per‑frame duration, so ffmpeg assumes 25 fps and then drops to your output rate.

I changed stitch_slab_pngs.py to write durations into the concat list and to use variable‑frame‑rate (-vsync vfr) so ffmpeg doesn’t drop frames. --fps now defines the base duration, and --frame-hold multiplies it.

Re‑run the same command (the script now computes durations internally):

python scripts/stitch_slab_pngs.py \
  --root outputs/quijote_batches_000_slabs \
  --png-suffix walls_3d.png \
  --combine-all \
  --output-dir outputs/quijote_batches_000_slabs/movies \
  --frame-hold 3 \
  --fps 15 \
  --overwrite

This should slow it down noticeably. If you still want slower, increase --frame-hold or reduce --fps (e.g., --fps 5 with --frame-hold 3).

I also updated the guide at docs/STITCH_SLAB_PNGS_USER_GUIDE.qmd to clarify how --frame-hold works.

The script is scripts/compute_density_field.py (typo in your name). It:

  • Reads a Gadget/Quijote HDF5 snapshot (--input) and a particle group (--parttype, default PartType1).
  • Streams particle coordinates in chunks and deposits them onto a 3D grid using CIC (cloud‑in‑cell).
  • Writes an output HDF5 file (--output) containing the density grid and metadata.
  • Optionally writes overdensity delta = rho/mean - 1 with --store-contrast.
  • Supports --mass-override if the snapshot’s MassTable is zero.

Outputs: - DensityField/<field_name> dataset (default density) - Optional DensityField/delta - Header attributes including GridSize, MeanDensity, FieldName

If you want, I can give you a quick usage example or add this to the docs.

05:03:57Z — user

can you explain to me what the CIC is and why it is useful to use/have?

05:04:08Z — assistant

CIC = Cloud‑in‑Cell. It’s a way to turn discrete particles into a smooth density field on a grid.

What it does - Each particle “spreads” its mass to the 8 surrounding grid cells (the corners of the cell it sits in). - The closer the particle is to a corner, the more weight that corner gets. - This avoids putting all the mass into a single cell (which would be noisy and grid‑dependent).

Why it’s useful - Smoother density field: Less shot noise than simple nearest‑grid assignment. - Better for derivatives: Gradients, Hessians, and topology methods behave better on a smooth field. - Preserves mass: Total mass is conserved across the grid. - Standard in cosmology: Widely used for power spectra, DTFE comparisons, and density/overdensity maps.

Compared to other schemes - NGP (nearest‑grid‑point): simplest but very blocky/noisy. - CIC: good balance of smoothness and speed. - TSC (triangular‑shaped cloud): smoother than CIC but more expensive.

In short: CIC gives you a more faithful, less noisy density grid for analysis, while staying fast enough to run on large snapshots.

05:05:24Z — user

so why am I using CIC and why is its output important? where does the ouput go?

05:05:33Z — assistant

You’re using CIC because you need a gridded density field from raw particle positions. Particles are discrete; most downstream analysis and visualization (maps, slices, contours, topology tools) require a continuous field on a grid. CIC gives that field in a stable, mass‑conserving way without excessive noise.

Why its output is important - It’s a smooth density grid that can be: - sliced, visualized, and exported, - compared against Delaunay/DTFE densities, - used for statistics (mean, contrast/overdensity), - used as input to other workflows that expect grid data.

Where the output goes - It’s written to an HDF5 file you specify with --output. - Inside that file: - DensityField/<field_name> contains the density grid. - Optional DensityField/delta contains overdensity if --store-contrast is used. - Header stores metadata (grid size, mean density, etc.).

So: CIC converts the particle snapshot into a regular 3D field, which becomes the bridge between raw simulation particles and grid‑based analysis/visualization.

05:14:20Z — user

The ND_TOPT_STATS_USER_GUIDE says, “Only filament IDs that match Delaunay IDs can contribute to scalar sums.”, can you please further clarify what you mean by this and what signifcance it holds?

05:14:33Z — assistant

That line means: we only add scalar values (mass/field/log‑field) for filament points that can be traced back to a real Delaunay vertex ID.

Why: - In ndtopo_stats.py, scalars come from the Delaunay NDnet (that’s the “ground truth” for mass/field values). - The filament skeleton contains interpolated points along arcs. Many of those points are not original Delaunay vertices. - When a filament point doesn’t match a Delaunay true_index, there is no reliable scalar value to use, so it’s excluded from scalar sums/means.

Significance: - Counts vs sums can diverge: filament counts include all skeleton points, but scalar sums only include those that map to Delaunay vertices. - This avoids inventing scalar values for interpolated points. - If you want all filament points to contribute, you’d need a different rule (e.g., interpolate scalars along the filament or use filament‑native fields rather than Delaunay).

So the statement is basically: “scalar totals are conservative and only based on original Delaunay vertices that the filament point can be traced back to.”

05:16:41Z — user

so tell me if i am wrong but what you mean to say that all filaments found from the skeleton arcs are counted but if the sums don’t match then they aren’t included in the total sum? So does that mean that the manifold filaments have a more acurate scaler sum because all of them match the delauany?

05:17:11Z — assistant

Short version:

  • Yes, all filament arc points are counted.
  • Scalar sums/means are computed only for the subset of those points that can be matched to a Delaunay true_index.
  • Unmatched filament points are dropped from the scalar totals, so the totals are effectively a lower bound on filament mass/field.

So it’s not that “if sums don’t match, then they aren’t included.” It’s that only the matched IDs are ever included in the sums.

About filament manifolds: they usually have a higher match rate because they come from NDnet (with true_index) rather than the skeleton’s interpolated arc points. That can make their scalar totals “more complete,” but it’s not guaranteed to be 100%—especially if you’re using smoothed VTK or if non‑0‑cells are involved.

If you want scalar totals to reflect all filament points, you’d need to interpolate scalars onto the skeleton (or use a different attribution rule).

*_topology_stats.csv

- walls_not_filaments, filaments_not_walls
- shared_walls_filaments, shared_walls_filament_manifolds, shared_filaments_filament_manifolds
- unassigned (none of the above)

    *_topology_points.csv
    One row per Delaunay point with boolean flags (is_wall, is_filament, is_filament_manifold) and scalars.

    _S000.vtu/.vtp for exact ID matching.

00:20:50Z — user

OK, I think I know what the problem is. The histogram bins are similarly sized, but for the field-value, most of the observations fall into the very first bin, since the distribution is extremely skewed. Would it be more appropriate to use a different logic to come up with histogram bins?

00:20:59Z — assistant

Yes. If the distribution is extremely skewed, equal‑width bins will collapse almost everything into the first bin. Better options:

  1. Quantile bins: choose bin edges so each bin has ~equal counts. This preserves structure across the full range and works well for skewed data.
  2. Log/transform bins: bin on log1p(field_value) or asinh(field_value) and label accordingly. This spreads out the tail without losing zeros.
  3. Adaptive bin width: Freedman–Diaconis or Scott’s rule on the transformed data can help, but still struggles if the raw scale is ultra‑skewed.
  4. Use raw values for violin/box: avoid hist‑based sampling entirely for those plots and compute stats directly from the per‑category raw values. This sidesteps the binning problem.

If you want, I can implement quantile‑based binning for field_value only, or switch the violin/box plots to use raw values while keeping histograms as they are.

01:21:32Z — assistant

Yes, that’s expected. The violin/box plots now ingest raw values per category, which means reading and materializing potentially hundreds of millions of points across all crops. That’s inherently slower and memory‑heavy compared to the previous histogram‑based approach.

If you want faster plots, you have a few options:

  1. Reservoir sample per category for plotting only
    Keep exact stats for CSVs, but build violins/boxes from (say) 50k–200k points per category.
    This keeps shapes accurate enough while staying fast.

  2. Histogram‑based approximation for violins/boxes
    Use the histogram counts to approximate the distribution (fastest), but it’s an approximation.

  3. Plot only a subset of crops
    Useful for quick iteration.

If you want, I can add a --plot-sample-size flag (default None = full raw, otherwise reservoir sampled) so you can trade speed vs fidelity without touching the stats.

22:31:18Z — assistant

That small shift is likely numerical noise from the alignment logic: we compute a translation based on min bounds, and tiny floating‑point differences can introduce a subtle offset. I added a tolerance clamp so sub‑millimetric shifts are forced to zero.

Specifically: - We now compute a tolerance tol = max(1e-6, 1e-6 * max_extent)
- Any |dx|, |dy|, |dz| below tol is set to 0 before applying the transform.

Please rerun the same command — the overlay should snap cleanly now.

If you still see a shift, I can add an explicit --png-align-debug flag to print bounds and computed shifts.

06:53:49Z — user

Filaments (both arc and manifold based ones) are hard to see. What do you recommend to make the lines thicker? Just tell me no need to change the code. (I reverted your last changes).

06:53:57Z — assistant

For visibility without code changes:

  1. Use arc filaments in composites
    The arc VTP is line‑like and responds well to thickness/opacity. Manifold filaments are surfaces and often blend into density.

  2. Max out filament opacity; reduce wall opacity
    Keep filaments at 1.0 and drop walls to ~0.3–0.5 so filaments stand out.

  3. Adjust the colormap/range for density
    Narrow the log density range so filaments aren’t washed out. For example, -3 to +1 with Inferno is good, but you can make it slightly darker (e.g. -2.5 to +0.5) to reduce background glare.

  4. Increase PNG resolution
    Higher resolution makes thin structures more visible. Try --png-dpi 600 or higher with larger base resolution.

  5. Toggle lighting off
    Lighting can add shading that hides thin features. With lighting off, colors read flatter and filaments pop more.

If you want a quick test run with these changes, I can suggest the exact batch_crop_and_clip.py flags.

05:11:31Z — user

can you remind me why we mapped the identifed manifold and filament results back to the original particles before obtaining the statistics?

05:11:44Z — assistant

We map manifolds/filaments back to the original particle indices so the statistics are computed on the same underlying Delaunay/particle scalars (mass, field_value, log_field_value). The skeleton/manifold outputs carry IDs that reference the original network; by matching those IDs to the Delaunay vertices we can:

  • aggregate per-particle scalars consistently across walls, filaments, and filament-manifolds,
  • avoid double-counting or mismatched scalar lookups,
  • and keep category overlap logic tied to the same universe of particle IDs.

Without the mapping, the sums/means would be computed on different index spaces and wouldn’t be comparable.

Internally it’s:

Higher zoom means the camera is closer because the orbit radius is divided by zoom. So: - Bigger zoom-peak → stronger “push‑in” - Bigger zoom-start → overall closer baseline

looking at the disperse readme (https://www.iap.fr/useriap/sousbie/web/html/index888d.html?archive) it seems that the mse computation does not have to be repeated for each export if all structures are saved in the msc file. then the msc file can just be reloaded for each dumping operation.

08:41:20Z — assistant

Yes — you’re reading the DisPerSE manual correctly. The manual says mse writes a backup .MSC and you can re‑run mse with -loadMSC to skip recomputation and still dump structures, as long as the MSC contains the needed geometry. (iap.fr)

Key limitation from the manual:

  • By default, the MSC does not store all manifolds geometry, so later -dumpManifolds can fail unless the initial run used -manifolds (to force storage of all manifolds) or the relevant manifolds were already dumped in that run. (iap.fr)
  • -loadMSC explicitly skips MS‑complex computation and is intended for fast re‑dumps. (iap.fr)

So the efficient pattern is:

  1. First mse run with -manifolds (and optionally -interArcsGeom if you need inter‑saddle arcs).
  2. Subsequent runs use -loadMSC <file.MSC> plus -dumpManifolds <TAG> or -dumpArcs ... as needed.

This avoids recomputing the MS complex and should be much faster. (iap.fr)

If you want, I can implement this in scripts/analyze_snapshot.py so that:

  • the first mse run uses -manifolds when multiple dumps are requested,
  • extra manifolds are dumped via -loadMSC,
  • and it falls back to the current behavior if the .MSC can’t be found.

That optimization is independent of your “cluster=0” issue (which is still almost certainly an ID‑field mismatch), but it will cut runtime a lot.

09:03:05Z — assistant

Short answer: the code is doing what it was designed to do, but your expectation (“clusters should exist because filaments connect maxima”) doesn’t guarantee that the cluster manifold IDs will match Delaunay vertex IDs.

Right now ndtopo_stats.py:

  • uses Delaunay point IDs (true_index) as the universe
  • and tries to match manifold IDs to those vertices.

That works for walls + filaments because their IDs often reference 0‑cells (vertices).
But J3a manifolds are 3‑manifolds, so their IDs often reference 3‑cells (tetrahedra), not vertices. If that’s the case, there is no overlap with Delaunay vertex IDs → cluster:0.

So this is not necessarily a bug — it’s a mapping mismatch.

How to confirm quickly

Please run this in the disperse environment (so vtkmodules is available):

python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa

path = Path("outputs/quijote_batches_000_slabs_w_clusters/crop_x500-1000_y0-500_z0-100/crop_x500-1000_y0-500_z0-100_s3_5_cluster_manifolds_J3a_S020.vtu")
r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader()
r.SetFileName(str(path)); r.Update()
d = dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

print("PointData arrays:", list(d.PointData.keys()))
print("CellData arrays:", list(d.CellData.keys()))

if "cell" in d.PointData:
    vals = d.PointData["cell"]
    frac = sorted(set(round(float(v) % 1, 1) for v in vals[:1000]))
    print("PointData cell fractional parts (sample):", frac)

if "cell" in d.CellData:
    vals = d.CellData["cell"]
    frac = sorted(set(round(float(v) % 1, 1) for v in vals[:1000]))
    print("CellData cell fractional parts (sample):", frac)
PY

If you see fractional parts like 0.3, that means 3‑cells → they will never match Delaunay vertex IDs (true_index).

If that’s the case, we need a new mapping mode

I can implement one of these:

Option A (fast)

Compute cluster stats from the cluster file’s own scalars, instead of Delaunay.
This avoids any mapping mismatch, but stats won’t be “Delaunay‑based”.

Option B (accurate, more work)

Compute a Delaunay cell scalar table (e.g. average of its 4 vertex scalars),
then match cluster IDs to Delaunay cell IDs.
This gives cluster stats consistent with Delaunay scalars.

What I already fixed
  • The slab crash is fixed (empty slabs now write a zero VTI instead of crashing).
  • ndtopo_stats.py now falls back through multiple ID fields and checks CellData arrays.
Tell me which mapping you want

If you want Option B (cell‑based mapping to Delaunay), I’ll implement it.
If you want Option A, that’s simpler.

Either way, J3a will then produce non‑zero cluster stats.

17:16:38Z — assistant

There is a very clear hint in your log — the cluster manifold export is empty. This line is the smoking gun:

Dumping geometry (2021 3-a) ...
3D-Network has 0 vertices.

So mse did compute maxima (2021 maxima), but when it tried to dump JE3a manifolds, the exported geometry contained zero vertices. That means:

  • the NDnet/VTU for JE3a has no points
  • so ndtopo_stats sees cluster:0
  • and any slab averaging will hit the empty‑data path

This is not an ID‑matching bug — the manifold file itself is empty.

Why this happens

In DisPerSE, 3‑manifolds are volumetric (not 0/1/2D geometry).
The NDnet/VTU export pipeline doesn’t have a representation for those volumes → it outputs zero vertices.

So you can absolutely have many filaments + maxima, but still get zero “cluster manifolds” in NDnet/VTU.

What you actually want for clusters

If you want clusters as points, you should export critical maxima (not the 3‑manifold geometry).

That’s consistent with your intuition: filaments connect saddles to maxima, so the maxima themselves are the cluster points.

Proposed fix (recommended)

Instead of dumping JE3a manifolds, add an option to export maxima critical points from the MSC (or from the skeleton) and include those in stats.

I can implement:

  • --dump-cluster-criticals (or similar)
  • Extract maxima critical points from the MSC / NDskl
  • Save them as a VTP/CSV and include in:
    • ndtopo_stats.py
    • per‑point CSV
    • slabs + PNG overlays

This would give you non‑empty cluster counts, consistent with the filament topology.

Additional bug I see (not asked but important)

Your run also shows this mismatch:

Expected file not found ..._manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu
...
Manifolds exported to ..._manifolds_J2a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu

That’s a naming collision bug in analyze_snapshot.py: it’s grabbing the wrong file when multiple “manifolds” files exist. I can fix that with a strict filename match (no wildcard confusion).

What I need from you

Do you want me to:

  1. implement maxima‑critical export as the “cluster” representation (recommended), and
  2. fix the manifolds naming collision so slabs don’t skip?

If yes, I’ll proceed.

02:57:35Z — user

before I say yes, what is the naming collision you refer to? I thought that the names are based on the inputs on the CLI.

02:57:53Z — assistant

Short answer: the collision isn’t in the CLI names — it’s in how our code constructs and later finds the converted VTU filenames when multiple manifold types exist.

Concrete example from your log:

  • We asked netconv to write J2a walls with an outName like ..._manifolds_J2a.

  • But the log shows it actually wrote:

    ..._manifolds_J2a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu

  • Later, batch_crop_and_clip.py looks for the expected file:

    ..._manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu

    and can’t find it → slabs skipped.

This happens because the conversion step and/or the lookup step is using pattern matching / string assembly that’s too loose, so when multiple “manifold” outputs exist (J2a, J1a, JE3a), the name can get polluted by another label (like filament_manifolds) or a glob picks the wrong file.

So the “collision” is: - Multiple manifold outputs share similar prefixes, and - The file-finding logic isn’t strict enough, so it sometimes grabs the wrong file or builds the wrong name.

The fix is to: 1. Make convert_manifolds(...) write a deterministic filename based on the exact tag (e.g., ..._manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu), and 2. Make any lookup use that exact tag, not a glob like *manifolds*J2a*.

That’s why I called it a naming collision: not the CLI names, but the code’s naming + matching of outputs once you have multiple manifold types in the same folder.

If you want, I can show you the exact lines in scripts/analyze_snapshot.py and scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py that are causing this.

04:08:32Z — assistant

Done. I implemented both fixes:

  1. Deterministic netconv output naming (manifolds + Delaunay):
    • If smoothing is enabled, the expected output is now ..._S###.vtu (exact), not a glob.
  2. Strict lookup when the exact file isn’t found:
    • The fallback now only accepts stems that match the exact base name (optionally with _S###), so it won’t accidentally grab a different manifold role (like filament manifolds).

These changes are in scripts/analyze_snapshot.py (both convert_manifolds and convert_network).

What to expect - The files should now be named exactly as batch_crop_and_clip.py expects, e.g.: crop_x..._s3_5_manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu - If you have stale, misnamed files from before, the new strict lookup won’t pick them up. It’s best to re-run or delete the old outputs for a clean test.

Files changed - scripts/analyze_snapshot.py

If you want, I can also tighten the NDnet selection in batch_crop_and_clip.py, but with this fix it should already align.

04:13:42Z — user

How about point 1 above: implement maxima‑critical export as the “cluster” representation (recommended)?

04:21:00Z — assistant

I’ve implemented maxima‑critical export as the default cluster representation and wired it into the pipeline, alongside the naming‑collision fix you already approved.

What changed

1) Maxima critical points export (clusters) - analyze_snapshot.py now generates a cluster critical‑points VTP by: - Running skelconv -to crits_ascii on the skeleton (prefer U, else first arc tag). - Parsing the .crits file and keeping only type=3 (maxima). - Mapping maxima points to Delaunay true_index using vtkPointLocator so they can be used in ndtopo_stats. - Writing *_cluster_critpoints_<TAG>_S000.vtp and adding it to the summary. - These critical points are also included in the summary stats CSV via summarize_vtk.

2) Pipeline uses the critical‑points clusters automatically - batch_crop_and_clip.py now searches for: - *cluster_critpoints*<TAG>*.vtp - If found, it uses that for ndtopo_stats and for slabs/PNGs. - It only falls back to the old NDnet cluster manifolds if the critpoints VTP is absent.

Files updated - scripts/analyze_snapshot.py - scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py

Notes / implications
  • The cluster representation now comes from maxima critical points, which is what you asked for.
  • The mapping to Delaunay uses nearest‑neighbor lookup in the Delaunay mesh and adds:
    • true_index
    • match_distance (distance between critical point and nearest Delaunay vertex)
  • If you run with no arcs, there’s no skeleton to pull critical points from, so clusters won’t export.
What to do next

Re‑run your existing command. You should now see:

  • A new file like:

    crop_x..._s3_5_cluster_critpoints_JE3a_S000.vtp

  • ndtopo_stats should report a non‑zero cluster count (assuming maxima exist).

  • Slab generation should include this cluster layer.

If you want, I can also: 1. Add a CLI flag to choose which arc tag supplies critical points. 2. Add a safeguard to warn if match_distance gets large (possible mapping mismatch).

Let me know if you want either of those.

06:55:24Z — assistant

Below is a clear, structure‑by‑structure explanation of how the workflow is identifying walls, filaments, and clusters in your run, and why each method is appropriate. I’ll use your exact tags and outputs in the explanation.

Big picture (common foundation)
All structures are derived from the same Morse–Smale complex computed by mse on the Delaunay‑DTFE density field built from your particles. That gives:

  • critical points (minima, saddles, maxima)
  • ascending/descending manifolds connecting them
  • arcs (1D connections) between critical points

This is the standard DisPerSE approach and makes the structures topologically consistent with each other.

1) Walls (sheet‑like structures)

How identified in your run - You requested: --dump-manifolds J2a - That means: ascending 2‑manifolds (2a) - Output:
..._s3.5_manifolds_J2a.NDnet

Why this makes sense - In 3D, ascending 2‑manifolds are sheet‑like surfaces (2D) that flow toward higher density. - These correspond to walls/sheets in the cosmic web.

2) Filaments (two complementary representations)
A) Arc filaments (skeleton)

How identified - You requested: --dump-arcs U - U = arcs leading to maxima - Output:
..._s3.5.U.NDskl

Why appropriate - These are the 1D ridge lines of the density field. - They directly connect saddles → maxima, which is a strong “filament spine” definition.

B) Filament manifolds (thickened filaments)

How identified - You requested: --dump-filament-manifolds J1a - That means: ascending 1‑manifolds (1D manifolds) - Output:
..._s3.5_manifolds_J1a.NDnet

Why appropriate - These are the continuous geometric manifolds associated with filamentary ridges. - Often provide a broader, more “tube‑like” filament representation than the skeleton arcs.

3) Clusters (maxima / nodes)
A) Manifold‑based cluster export (what DisPerSE gives)

How identified - You requested: --dump-cluster-manifolds JE3a - That means: extended ascending 3‑manifolds - Output:
..._s3.5_manifolds_JE3a.NDnet - In your log this export has 0 vertices.

Why it doesn’t work here - 3‑manifolds are volumes, not point sets. In many DisPerSE runs they don’t export as vertices, so you get an empty NDnet. - This is why your earlier “zero clusters” happened.

B) Maxima critical points (what we now use)

How identified - We now export critical points from the skeleton using skelconv -to crits_ascii. - We filter to type=3 (maxima) only. - These are then mapped to Delaunay true_index using nearest‑neighbor lookup, and saved as: ..._cluster_critpoints_JE3a_S000.vtp

Why appropriate - Clusters in DisPerSE correspond to maxima of the density field. - Maxima are the most direct and stable definition of “nodes” in the web. - This approach gives actual point locations, which can be matched back to Delaunay particles and used in your stats pipeline.

Summary: how they differ & why each is right
Structure Identification method Tag used Output Why appropriate
Walls Ascending 2‑manifolds J2a NDnet/VTU surface 2D sheets in 3D are walls
Filaments (skeleton) Arcs to maxima U NDskl/VTP lines 1D ridge lines define filament spine
Filaments (manifolds) Ascending 1‑manifolds J1a NDnet/VTU Provides thicker, manifold‑based filaments
Clusters (nodes) Maxima critical points derived from crits_ascii VTP points Maxima are natural cluster definition; manifold 3‑volumes export empty
Important observation from your log

You’re now correctly getting 2021 clusters:

[info] Loaded ids -> ... cluster:2021 (true_index)

That confirms the maxima‑critical export is working.

If you want, I can also add a short explanation block like this to the user guide and the workflow flowchart so it’s documented for future runs.

07:04:56Z — user

Is there any other way to extract the clusters besides going through the crits_ascii file? Doesn’t something similar to the other structures work? No need to change anything just explain.

07:05:11Z — assistant

Short answer: in DisPerSE, “clusters” are fundamentally critical points (maxima), so there isn’t a clean “surface/line manifold” export that behaves like walls or filaments and still gives you usable point IDs. The alternatives all end up being either volumetric or implicit, which is why the crits export is the most practical.

Here are the main options and why they’re not as usable as crits:

1) Ascending 3‑manifolds (J3a / JE3a)

This is the closest analog to walls (J2a) or filament manifolds (J1a), but:

  • It represents 3‑dimensional volumes (entire basins flowing into maxima).
  • For many datasets it exports as empty geometry (0 vertices), which is what you observed.
  • Even when it doesn’t export empty, it’s volumetric, not a “node” set.

So it doesn’t behave like a clean “cluster point set”.

2) Use arcs to maxima (skeleton U)

You can infer clusters from the endpoints of skeleton arcs:

  • The endpoints are maxima.
  • But the NDskl format is primarily line geometry, not a point catalog.
  • Extracting endpoints is doable, but DisPerSE doesn’t export them directly as a point list with Delaunay IDs. You would still need a conversion step (very similar to what crits_ascii provides).

So it’s not simpler than crits.

3) MSC file directly

The MSC contains all critical points, but:

  • It’s not directly readable without DisPerSE tools.
  • You still need a conversion step to extract the maxima (which is what skelconv -to crits_ascii effectively does).
Why crits_ascii is used
  • It’s the only standard DisPerSE export that explicitly lists critical points with their type (0/1/2/3).
  • It gives you a direct way to select maxima (type=3).
  • It’s portable, easy to parse, and you can map to Delaunay IDs.

Bottom line
If you want clusters as points, the critical‑point export is the most faithful and practical DisPerSE‑native method. Manifold exports work well for walls and filament manifolds, but clusters are not a manifold of lower dimension—they are 0‑dimensional maxima, so critical‑point export is the correct representation.

07:09:21Z — user

I noticed in paraview that field value is but log field values is not exported as a scalar associated with clusters. Is that intentional?

07:09:31Z — assistant

Yes — that’s currently intentional, and it’s because the cluster points are coming from the critical‑point export, not from a VTK dataset that already carries all scalars.

Here’s why:

  • The crits_ascii file only includes one scalar value per critical point: the raw field_value from DisPerSE.
  • It does not include log_field_value.
  • When we build the cluster VTP, we only have what’s in the crits file, so we attach:
    • field_value
    • plus metadata like crit_type, pair_id, boundary, and true_index.

So the absence of log_field_value on clusters is expected with this method.

If you want log_field_value attached to clusters, there are two possible approaches:

  1. Compute it locally in the cluster VTP (e.g., log(field_value)), or
  2. Sample it from the Delaunay mesh at the mapped true_index.

Both are straightforward to add, but right now we intentionally kept clusters minimal and faithful to what DisPerSE outputs directly.

07:11:03Z — user

How do other structures get their log-field value? Using option 1 or 2 above?

07:11:16Z — assistant

For the other structures (walls, filament manifolds, filament arcs), the log_field_value is already carried in the DisPerSE outputs, so we’re not computing it or sampling it.

In other words: neither option 1 nor 2 is used for those.

Specifically:

  • NDnet / NDskl outputs from mse already include:
    • field_value
    • log_field_value
    • mass
    • plus indexing arrays (index, true_index, etc.)

So when we convert those to VTU/VTP (via netconv/skelconv), the arrays are preserved and appear in ParaView automatically.

Why clusters are different

Clusters are derived from critical point export (crits_ascii), which only contains the raw field value (plus type, pairing info, etc.), so it does not include log_field_value to begin with.

If you want, I can add log_field_value for clusters by: - Option 1: computing log(field_value) directly in the cluster VTP, or - Option 2: pulling log_field_value from the Delaunay mesh using the mapped true_index.

Both are simple — just say which you prefer.

07:12:15Z — user

Woudl the two options produce the same log-field value?

07:12:24Z — assistant

They should be very close, but not guaranteed to be identical.

Here’s why:

Option 1: log(field_value) from crits
  • Uses the exact field value that DisPerSE assigns to the critical point.
  • You compute log on that value directly.
Option 2: sample log_field_value from Delaunay
  • Uses the nearest Delaunay vertex (mapped via true_index) and reads its log_field_value.
  • That vertex is usually the same one where the critical point sits, but not always.
  • Any small mismatch in mapping (or discretization) can give a slightly different log value.
Practical implication
  • If the critical point is exactly at a Delaunay vertex, both are identical.
  • If it’s not, Option 2 gives you the log_field_value of the nearest vertex, which can differ slightly.

If you want the value most faithful to DisPerSE’s critical point, Option 1 is the better choice.
If you want consistency with the Delaunay scalar field, Option 2 is more consistent with the other structures.

now, when you look at the output folder, you will see that several files are written with _S020 and .S020 as well as _S000 and .S000, that is an underscore separator or a dot separator. Why is that?

07:25:17Z — assistant

That’s expected and comes from two different DisPerSE tools using different naming conventions, not from your CLI tags:

1) mse / netconv use underscore separators

These tools produce names like:

..._S020.vtu

because our wrapper builds names with _S###, and netconv honors that.

Example:

crop_x..._s3_5_manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu
2) skelconv uses dot separators

skelconv always appends its smoothing token with a dot:

... .S020.vtp

Example:

crop_x..._s3_5_arcs_U.S020.vtp

It does this internally, and we don’t override it.

3) crits_ascii also uses dot separators

skelconv -to crits_ascii writes:

... .S000.a.crits

Again, this is skelconv’s internal format, not ours.

Summary
Tool Smoothing token format
netconv (manifolds, Delaunay) _S###
skelconv (arcs, crits) .S###

So you’ll see both styles in the output folder because they come from different tools with different built‑in filename conventions.

If you want, I can normalize everything after the fact (rename to one consistent style), but I’ve kept the native naming because the tools themselves expect those patterns.

You’re right to call this out. The dot vs underscore difference is not coming from your CLI; it’s coming from tool‑level naming, plus our normalization logic. Here’s what’s actually happening:

Why both exist
1) netconv and skelconv append .S### (dot)

When smoothing is applied, both tools internally append the smoothing token with a dot:

... .S020.vtu
... .S020.vtp

So crop_x..._filament_manifolds_J1a.S020.vtu is the native tool output.

2) Our code normalizes names to _S###

We run everything through sanitize_filename(...), which converts dots inside the stem to underscores.
So the same file becomes:

... _S020.vtu
3) You now have both because they came from different runs

If: - a run created the dot version, and - another run (or our rename) created the underscore version,

they coexist because they’re different filenames.

That’s why you see both:

..._J1a.S020.vtu
..._J1a_S020.vtu
Why this is currently causing confusion

You also have this warning in the log:

[warn] netconv output name mismatch; using ..._S000.vtu instead of ..._S020.vtu

That happens because our strict matching only looks for _S###, but netconv produced .S020, which we ignored, so we fell back to an old _S000 file.

So the dot/underscore mismatch isn’t just cosmetic — it can lead to using the wrong smoothing level.

Summary
  • Dot .S020 = raw tool output
  • Underscore _S020 = normalized/renamed output
  • Seeing both means multiple runs or partial renames.

If you want, I can do one of the following:

  1. Adjust the matcher to accept .S###, then rename it to _S### (so only one remains).
  2. Skip renaming entirely and just use the tool’s native .S### naming.

Either would stop the duplicates and avoid the warning you saw.

but these are not direct duplicates (or only renames) because the file sizes are significantly different. why?

That’s because they are not just renames — they’re different outputs from different smoothing levels or different runs, and the name ambiguity let both coexist.

Specifically:

  2. Our code then tries to find the expected _S### name, and if it doesn’t exist it falls back to whatever match it can find.

So you can end up with:

  • .S020 file = the current smoothed output from the tool
  • _S020 file = an older or renamed output from a previous run
  • or _S000 = a fallback from a different run entirely

Since they’re produced in different runs (sometimes with different smoothing or data), their sizes can be very different.

That’s exactly what your log showed:

[warn] ... using ..._S000.vtu instead of ..._S020.vtu

So the size difference is a symptom of: - multiple runs, and - file lookup mismatch (dot vs underscore), causing the pipeline to sometimes load the wrong output.

Bottom line:
The dot/underscore mismatch is causing file selection drift across runs, so you see multiple non‑identical files with similar names.

07:54:22Z — assistant

Thanks — the failure is exactly because netconv writes .S020 (dot form), and my strict matcher was only accepting _S020.

I’ve now updated the matcher to accept both _S### and .S###:

  • It will find either form, then
  • sanitize_filename() will normalize the dot to underscore, so only one consistent name remains.

This should fix the crash and prevent the wrong file from being selected.

Updated file - scripts/analyze_snapshot.py

If you rerun the workflow now, it should find the .S020 file, normalize it, and proceed without errors.

08:04:05Z — assistant

You’re hitting the error because persistence_tag sometimes ends up None, so the code expects a filename without the _s3_5_ segment. That makes the strict matcher miss the real file:

crop_x..._s3_5_manifolds_J2a.S020.vtu

I’ve now updated the matcher to handle that case:

✅ What I changed

In scripts/analyze_snapshot.py:

  • If the strict match fails and no persistence tag is available, it now falls back to a safe substring match that still respects the manifold role (and avoids grabbing filament/cluster manifolds).
  • It also accepts both _S### and .S###.

So even if persistence isn’t detected, the file is still found and normalized.

What you should see now

The run should complete, and the dot name will be normalized to underscore:

..._s3_5_manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu

If you want, I can also add a debug print of base_name + persistence_tag to make this easier to diagnose next time.

08:26:29Z — assistant

Thanks — this failure was still because the matcher only used the “exact base_name” and didn’t fall back when that base_name existed but didn’t match the on‑disk filename. I’ve now made the fallback always run when strict matching fails, regardless of whether a persistence tag was found.

What changed

In scripts/analyze_snapshot.py:

  • If strict matching fails, it now always tries a broader search for:
    • _{role}_..._{tag}
    • It still avoids confusing manifolds with filament_manifolds and cluster_manifolds.

This makes it robust to all the dot/underscore variants and oddities.

Next step

Please re‑run the same command again. It should now find:

..._manifolds_J2a.S020.vtu

and normalize it to:

..._manifolds_J2a_S020.vtu

so the pipeline can proceed.

If you want, I can also add a short debug print of: - base_name - expected_name - matched file

so you can see exactly what it picked in the logs.

04:32:22Z — user

What does the –dump-cluster-manifolds argument actually accomplish? Does it dump cluster manifolds (from and NDnet file)? Or does it dump clusters from skeletons (from and NDskl file)?

04:32:37Z — assistant

Short answer: --dump-cluster-manifolds tells mse to dump cluster manifolds into an NDnet (via -dumpManifolds <TAG>), and in our pipeline it also triggers an extra export of cluster critical points (maxima) as VTP/VTU for downstream analysis. It does not dump clusters from the NDskl arcs.

More detail: - From NDnet (manifolds): mse ... -dumpManifolds <TAG> writes <prefix>_sX_manifolds_<TAG>.NDnet and then netconv can convert that to VTU. This is the “cluster manifolds” output, and it is often empty for J3a/JE3a after smoothing. - From critical points (maxima): when --dump-cluster-manifolds is set, we also export cluster critical points (maxima) to <prefix>_cluster_critpoints_<TAG>_S000.vtp/.vtu. This is the primary cluster representation used by ndtopo_stats.py.

So the flag does both: it requests a manifolds NDnet from mse, and it triggers the critical‑point (maxima) export for clusters.

04:35:07Z — user

OK, are the critical points based on NDnet or NDskl files? Or are they coming from the MSC file?

04:35:31Z — assistant

They come from the NDskl (skeleton), via skelconv -to crits_ascii. We don’t read the MSC directly.

Pipeline-wise: - mse builds the MSC and writes an NDskl (skeleton). - We run skelconv on that NDskl to export crits_ascii. - We then filter type=3 (maxima) to define clusters.

So: not NDnet, not directly MSC, but NDskl-derived (which itself is produced from the MSC).

04:36:14Z — user

So the critical points are not actually based on manifolds, right? And therefore clusters aren’t either, right?

04:36:17Z — assistant

Correct. The cluster critical points are not derived from manifolds. They come from the skeleton/MSC critical points (maxima), extracted via skelconv -to crits_ascii on the NDskl.

So: - Clusters (as we use them) = maxima critical points from the MSC/skeleton. - Not from manifold geometry.

04:36:46Z — user

So this arguemnt name is misleading, right? –dump-cluster-manifolds

04:36:50Z — assistant

It is a bit misleading in practice, yes. The flag name suggests “manifolds,” but in our pipeline it also triggers the cluster critical‑point export, which is what we actually use downstream. The true manifold dump still happens (from NDnet), but it’s often empty, so the usable “cluster” output is the critical points.

04:38:25Z — user

04:38:30Z — assistant

Yes, that would make sense and be clearer for users.

Pragmatically, I’d recommend: - Add a new --dump-clusters flag that only triggers the critical‑point (maxima) export. - Keep --dump-cluster-manifolds as a backward‑compatible alias (maybe deprecated in help text), so existing scripts don’t break.

If you want, I can implement that rename+alias and update the docs/examples accordingly.

05:56:11Z — user

what is the tag here: –dump-clusters

05:56:28Z — assistant

It’s just a label for the cluster critical‑points export. Use the same DisPerSE-style tag you want to associate with clusters (e.g., JE3a or J3a) so filenames and batch matching are consistent.

Important details: - The tag does not change which points are exported. We still take all maxima from the skeleton; the tag is only used in naming. - You still need --dump-arcs (or --skel-input) because the critical points are extracted from the NDskl.

Example:

--dump-clusters JE3a

produces: <prefix>_cluster_critpoints_JE3a_S000.vtp/.vtu

05:58:10Z — user

but since clusers are not manifold based, what is the point of the tag? the JE3a tag is a manifold tag.

05:58:19Z — assistant

You’re right: the clusters we export are not manifold‑based, so the tag is just a label. It has two purposes:

  1. Filename/organization – it becomes part of the output name:
    <prefix>_cluster_critpoints_<TAG>_S000.vtp/.vtu
  2. Matching in batch workflows – batch_crop_and_clip.py looks for that tag to pick up the right file.

So the tag doesn’t affect the data, only the naming and downstream matching.
Use anything consistent. Recommended options:

  • Keep JE3a (or J3a) if you want continuity with your MSE tagging style.
  • Or use something neutral like maxima or clusters if you want to avoid manifold semantics.

06:00:27Z — assistant

Yes, the filename already includes cluster_critpoints, so the tag is not strictly necessary. We kept it for two practical reasons:

  1. Disambiguation: If you generate multiple cluster exports in the same folder (different persistence, boundary choices, or runs), the tag keeps them from colliding.
  2. Batch matching: The batch scripts currently look for a tag in the filename to select the right file.

If you prefer, we can make the tag optional (e.g., --dump-clusters with no tag or a default like clusters) and adjust the batch matching to accept the no‑tag filename. Want me to do that?

1) Why ..._manifolds_J1a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu has the extra “manifolds”

That file is created by our unsmoothed conversion step (via ndtopo_stats.py --write-vtk or when we convert NDnet → VTU). The NDnet file is:

crop_..._s3_5_manifolds_J1a.NDnet

When we convert it, we preserve the original stem (..._manifolds_J1a) and append a role label (filament_manifolds) so the VTU name clearly indicates what it represents. That’s why you get:

..._manifolds_J1a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu

It’s redundant, but it avoids collisions and makes the role explicit.

If you want shorter names, we can simplify that naming rule.

2) Why the .crits file has dots:
crop_..._s3_5_cluster_critpoints_J3a.S000.a.crits

This filename comes directly from skelconv -to crits_ascii, which uses the DisPerSE convention:

<base>.S000.a.crits

So the dots are not from our code — they’re DisPerSE’s native naming for the ASCII critical‑point dump. We then read that file and write the cleaned outputs:

..._cluster_critpoints_J3a_S000.vtp/.vtu
3) Why you have both _S000 and _S020
  • _S020 files are the smoothed conversions from netconv/skelconv in analyze_snapshot.py.
  • _S000 files are unsmoothed conversions created by ndtopo_stats.py --write-vtk.

So it’s normal to see both when you run both steps.

Even though clusters are not manifold‑based, we keep the tag in the name so: - batch scripts can find the right file, and - multiple runs won’t collide.

But you’re right: the tag does not affect the data. It’s purely a label.

    So the converter adds the role label:

    ..._manifolds_J1a  →  ..._manifolds_J1a_filament_manifolds_S000.vtu

So the “extra words” only show up when the role isn’t obvious from the base stem (filament manifolds, cluster manifolds). Walls are already obvious, so no extra suffix is added.

Here’s what you’re seeing:

1) The two subfolders

These are ParaView multiblock directories.
When batch_clip.py writes a .vtm file, ParaView saves the .vtm plus a sibling folder that contains the referenced blocks.

So you’ll see pairs like: - crop_..._walls_filaments.vtm - crop_..._walls_filaments/
and similarly for the “filament_manifolds_cluster_manifolds” multiblock.

What’s inside the folders?
They contain the actual per‑block VTK pieces referenced by the .vtm file. The .vtm is just a “table of contents”; the folder is the actual data.

2) Why cluster manifold files look empty

Because those “cluster manifolds” are critical points (VTP with points), not surfaces.
If you view them as surfaces or expect geometry thickness, they look empty.

Specific reasons they can look empty: - They are just points, not surfaces/lines. - The slab clip can remove most/all points if none fall inside the slab thickness. - If you open the flattened (*_cluster_manifolds.vtp) without glyphing, the points can be invisible.

Try this in ParaView: - Open *_cluster_manifolds_3d.vtp - Set Representation = Points - Increase Point Size - Or apply Glyph (Sphere)

You should see the points if any fall into the slab.

3) What each “avg.vti” is

Those *_avg.vti files are resampled/averaged 2D grids for each structure (walls/filaments/cluster/filament manifolds).
They’re only used if you want to treat the topology as a density‑like raster; otherwise you can ignore them.

If you want, I can: - stop writing .vtm multiblocks (and the folders), - skip the *_avg.vti grids for non‑density objects, - or stop writing any of the cluster slab outputs unless you explicitly enable them.

08:57:50Z — user

can you remind me why is the count and mass_sum of manifolds different in the crop topology stats file? for all other topologies the count and mass_sum match.

08:57:58Z — assistant

Because the count and mass_sum measure different things:

  • count = number of IDs (Delaunay vertices) that fall into the category.
  • mass_sum = sum of the mass scalar on those Delaunay vertices.

So they only “match” numerically if each vertex has mass = 1.
For most categories in your run, mass behaves close to a constant per vertex, so count ≈ mass_sum.
For manifolds, the selected IDs are biased toward higher‑density regions, so the mass per vertex is larger on average, and mass_sum diverges from count.

In short:
Manifold membership is correlated with higher mass values, so mass_sum is larger even though the number of IDs (count) isn’t.

08:59:18Z — user

can you remind me why is the count and mass_sum of filaments different in the crop topology stats file? for all other topologies the count and mass_sum match. and the mass for all of them is 1.

08:59:34Z — assistant

It’s because filament IDs include many points that don’t map to any Delaunay vertex, even though mass = 1 for the Delaunay vertices.

In ndtopo_stats.py: - count = number of filament IDs coming from the skeleton (NDskl, via the cell array). - mass_sum = sum of Delaunay mass only for IDs that actually exist in the Delaunay mesh.

Filament skeletons are densely sampled along arcs; many of those samples are interpolated points whose cell IDs don’t correspond to a Delaunay true_index. Those still count toward count, but they don’t contribute to mass_sum, so mass_sum < count.

If you want count to match mass_sum for filaments, use only valid 0‑cell IDs:

--filaments-cell-mode zero

That keeps only exact integer cell IDs (the actual critical points), so every filament ID should map to Delaunay and the sums will line up.

in the new table, when the scalar is not a manifold (i.e it is a filament or cluster) the mass is zero. why?

16:45:15Z — assistant

Because the filament and cluster datasets don’t carry a mass array.

In the new “topology‑scalars” table we read scalars from the topology files themselves:

  • Filaments (from NDskl/VTP) typically only have geometry + cell/IDs and maybe topology_type, not mass.
  • Cluster critical points we create ourselves, and we only write field_value and log_field_value (no mass).

So when the table tries to aggregate mass from those files, there’s nothing to read, and it defaults to 0.

If you want non‑zero mass there, we have a few options: 1. Map mass from Delaunay for filaments/clusters (similar to the main stats table). 2. Populate mass into the topology datasets when we export them (more work, but cleaner). 3. Drop mass from the topology‑scalar table (or only keep scalars that exist).

Tell me which you prefer and I’ll implement it.

Why?

04:24:29Z — assistant

Short answer:

  • .S020 is the filename convention DisPerSE itself uses when you pass -smooth 20 to netconv/skelconv. It inserts the smooth tag with a dot.
  • Our pipeline normalizes that to _S020 so it’s easier to parse/consistently grep, using sanitize_filename() in scripts/analyze_snapshot.py.
    If you still see both forms, it means the dot‑version was produced in a previous run and not cleaned up, or the rename didn’t occur (best‑effort rename can fail silently). The underscore and dot files should be equivalent, but if their sizes differ, they’re likely from different runs (different parameters or older artifacts), not true duplicates from the same run.

Why you see _S000:

  • _S000 is explicit “unsmoothed” output. We create these in the stats/analysis stage (e.g., ndtopo_stats.py uses -smooth 0 when exporting unsmoothed VTKs for the CSVs). These are intentional and separate from the smoothed S020 visualization meshes.

So in practice: - Use *_S020 for smoothed visualization products. - Use *_S000 for unsmoothed/statistical outputs. - If you want only one naming style, we can add a cleanup step that removes .S### variants after renaming, or we can write everything to a clean output directory each run.

If you want me to add an automatic cleanup, say the word and I’ll implement it.

04:40:06Z — assistant

Here’s what the code does right now:

  • analyze_snapshot.py never writes S000. It only writes smoothed outputs when --netconv-smooth / --skelconv-smooth > 0 (your runs use 20), so it produces only _S020 files.
    See convert_manifolds() / convert_network() in scripts/analyze_snapshot.py — they only append S### when smooth_iters > 0.

  • S000 is only created by ndtopo_stats.py, and only when it is given NDnet/NDskl and --write-vtk is used. That script converts to unsmoothed VTK with -smooth 0 and names it _S000.
    See ensure_vtu_from_ndnet() / ensure_vtp_from_ndskl() in scripts/ndtopo_stats.py.

So if you don’t see any _S000 now, it means one of these is true:

  1. You’re looking at the slab folder (it never writes S000; it writes *_z0_* outputs only).
  2. ndtopo_stats.py didn’t run or ran with VTK inputs (so no conversion).
  3. The --write-vtk conversion step was skipped (not in your current run, but if you ran stats differently).

If you want me to make sure S000 always gets emitted in the crop folder (or never, by cleaning them up), I can adjust that.

21:03:09Z — user

but what is the downside of streaming?

21:03:18Z — assistant

The streaming engine is approximate for plots/histograms and some quantile‑based outputs. Specifically:

  • Stats (count, sum, mean, min, max) are exact.
  • Std/variance is exact (computed online).
  • Histograms/quantiles/violin/box are approximate, because streaming only keeps a reservoir sample (default 20,000) to estimate quantiles and bins.

So the downside is less precise distribution shapes and quantiles. If you only care about aggregate counts and means, streaming is fine; if you need accurate tails/quantiles, use Polars or split‑and‑merge.

If you want streaming but with higher precision, we can increase the reservoir sample size (at some memory cost).

How can I make Log_{10} follow latex rules so that the {} shows up as a subscript?

22:09:18Z — assistant

Use Matplotlib’s mathtext: wrap the label in $...$ and use \log_{10}. Example:

ax.set_ylabel(r'$\log_{10}$ Density')
ax.set_title(r'$\log_{10}$ Density distribution by category')

If you want it literally “Log” (capital L) instead of the log symbol:

ax.set_ylabel(r'$Log_{10}$ Density')

The $...$ is what makes the {10} render as a subscript.

Short answer: delaunay.vtu is produced by running DisPerSE’s delaunay_3D on your particle catalog and then converting the resulting .NDnet to VTK with netconv.

Process flow (from raw snapshot to delaunay.vtu) 1. Load snapshot particles (PartType1) from data/snapdir_XXX. 2. Crop / stride the particles (your --crop-box and --stride). 3. Write NDfield catalog (*_coords_stride*.AND) with particle positions. 4. Build Delaunay tessellation with DisPerSE: - delaunay_3D <coords.AND> -outName <prefix> -outDir <dir> -btype <periodic|...> - Output: <prefix>.NDnet 5. Convert NDnet to VTK: - netconv <prefix>.NDnet -outName <prefix>_delaunay -outDir <dir> -to vtu - Output: <prefix>_delaunay.vtu

In your pipeline This is handled inside scripts/analyze_snapshot.py when --export-delaunay is set (your batch_crop_and_clip.py passes that). The logs show: - Writing *_coords_stride1.AND - Running delaunay_3D - Running netconv to write *_delaunay.vtu

17:47:45Z — user

does the delaunay 3d step carry out any interpolation? in other words does the tessalation still contain the original particle positions or are there also interpolated positions too?

17:47:51Z — assistant

No interpolation is performed by delaunay_3D.

It builds a Delaunay tessellation using your input particle positions as the vertices. The resulting .NDnet stores:

  • the original particle coordinates (as vertices)
  • the connectivity (edges/triangles/tetrahedra) between those points
  • any fields assigned at vertices (e.g., field_value, log_field_value, mass)

So the tessellation contains only the original particle positions, not interpolated points. The interpolation happens later only if you explicitly resample to a grid (e.g., in the slab step when you build *.vti).

If you’re seeing a grid, the most likely causes are:

  1. You opened a resampled density grid, not the point cloud.
    The VTI files like *_density_3d.vti or *_density_avg.vti are regular grids and will look perfectly uniform.

  2. You loaded the right file but ParaView is showing a different pipeline output (e.g., a resampled volume or an image).

  3. You’re looking at delaunay_S000.vtu in “Surface” mode, which only shows the boundary of the unstructured grid.
    For point clouds, the representation should be Points (or Point Gaussian) on the *_delaunay_point_S000.vtp/.vtu file.

If you want to sanity‑check that the file itself isn’t a grid, run this quick check (replace the filename):

python - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLPolyDataReader

path = "outputs/.../crop_x..._delaunay_point_S000.vtp"
r = vtkXMLPolyDataReader(); r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
poly = r.GetOutput()
pts = np.array([poly.GetPoint(i) for i in range(poly.GetNumberOfPoints())])

for i, axis in enumerate("xyz"):
    vals = np.unique(pts[:, i])
    diffs = np.unique(np.round(np.diff(np.sort(vals)), 6))
    print(axis, "unique:", len(vals), "diffs sample:", diffs[:10])
PY

If you see lots of unique values and many different diffs, it’s not a grid.

after i take a box type slice in paraview, i can’t see the contents of the slice or the points inside. why?

19:58:49Z — assistant

This is usually one of two things:

  1. A slice has zero thickness
    Your point cloud is 0‑D (vertices). A plane slice has zero volume, so it often hits no points and shows empty output.
    Fix: use a box/clip with thickness or a threshold instead of a plane slice.

  2. Clip without “Crinkle Clip” drops points
    For point data, the standard Clip may operate on cells and can return nothing.
    Fix: in the Clip filter, check “Crinkle clip” so it clips points.

Try this in ParaView - Load *_delaunay_point_S000.vtp (or .vtu), set Representation = Points or Point Gaussian, increase point size. - Use Clip → Box, enable “Crinkle clip”, and make sure Inside Out is correct. - Alternatively use Extract Points or Extract Selection with a box.

If you tell me exactly which file and which filter you’re using (Clip vs Slice vs Extract), I can give a precise fix.

what is the size of the whiskers in the boxplot?

02:26:11Z — assistant

They’re 1.5×IQR (Tukey). In code:

  • whislo = max(min, q1 - 1.5 * IQR)
  • whishi = min(max, q3 + 1.5 * IQR)

So it uses the standard 1.5×IQR rule, clipped to the observed min/max.

Option B: Export 4 separate VTUs

Pros - Zero ParaView pipeline setup - Clear separation

Here’s what the CSV columns mean and which scalar space they’re in.

Columns (for each category)

The file is *_topology_stats.csv. Each row is one category.

Which log space is used?
  • field_value

    • If you run with --log10-field-value, then field_value is converted to log10 before stats are computed.

  • log_field_value
    Always natural log (ln) from the input data.
    It is not affected by --log10-field-value.

Column prefix Meaning
field_value_* raw density (or log10 if --log10-field-value)
log_field_value_* natural log density

Next thing I want you to change is the stats. I found an inconsistency with the feild value. Are you sure those are actual densities or is there some transformation already on them?

06:58:40Z — assistant

Short answer: field_value in the stats is whatever DisPerSE wrote into the Delaunay mesh (*_delaunay*.vtu/NDnet) and we do not transform it in ndtopo_stats.py. It is the DTFE density estimate (i.e., derived from the Delaunay/Voronoi cell volume), not a log. The only log in the Delaunay data is log_field_value, which is already present in the NDnet/VTU and is natural log.

Here’s the evidence in code:

  • ndtopo_stats.py reads scalars directly from the Delaunay mesh and writes them as-is (no transforms).
  • It uses whatever is in the VTK point data for field_value and log_field_value.
  • The aggregate script only adds log10_field_value as a new column; it does not overwrite field_value.

If you want a quick sanity check on a Delaunay file, run this:

python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa

vtu = Path("outputs/quijote_batches_000_w_clusters/crop_x500-1000_y0-500_z0-100/crop_x500-1000_y0-500_z0-100_delaunay.vtu")
r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader()
r.SetFileName(str(vtu))
r.Update()
d = dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())
f = np.array(d.PointData["field_value"])
lf = np.array(d.PointData["log_field_value"])
mask = f > 0
err = np.nanmean(np.abs(np.log(f[mask]) - lf[mask]))
print("mean |ln(field_value) - log_field_value| =", err)
print("field_value range:", f.min(), f.max())
print("log_field_value range:", lf.min(), lf.max())
PY

If the mean error is ~0, then: - field_value is raw density - log_field_value is natural log density

Why: - batch_crop_and_clip.py defaults to --input-unit kpc/h and --output-unit mpc/h. - The crop box is interpreted in input units (kpc/h), then converted by unit_scale() (0.001) to output units (mpc/h) before writing the NDfield catalog and running delaunay_3D.

So in your command:

This becomes:

  • 500000 kpc/h = 500 Mpc/h
  • 100000 kpc/h = 100 Mpc/h

Thus the Delaunay mesh (and all its volumes) are in Mpc/h, and volumes are in (Mpc/h)^3.

If you want the tessellation (and volumes) to stay in kpc/h, run:

--output-unit kpc/h

(Keep --input-unit kpc/h unless your snapshot coordinates are already in Mpc/h.)

00:49:28Z — user

what does the aggregate_topology_points.py script do?

00:49:59Z — assistant

Here’s a summary of what aggregate_topology_points.py does:

Purpose

Aggregates per-point topology CSV files (produced by ndtopo_stats.py --per-point-csv) across multiple spatial “crops” into combined summary statistics and histogram outputs.

Core workflow

  1. Input discovery — finds all *_topology_points.csv files, either via a glob under --root or an explicit --inputs list.

  2. Aggregation (three engine choices):

    • polars (default, fast) — uses the Polars dataframe library; supports chunked processing to reduce memory.
    • python (exact, slower) — pure Python, loads everything into memory.
    • stream (approximate) — streaming pass, trading exactness for lower memory.

  3. Categories — points are classified into topology categories representing cosmic web structures:

    • Clusters, Filaments, Walls, Unassigned
    • Also handles a finer breakdown with filament_manifold and cluster_manifold flags.

  4. Statistics computed per category — count, sum, mean, min, Q25, median, Q75, max, std, skew for scalar fields (primarily field_value / density and its log transforms).

  5. Outputs written:

    • *_topology_stats.csv — main summary stats table.
    • *_topology_stats_transforms.csv — same stats in a long/tidy format per scalar transform.
    • Histogram CSVs per scalar × category.
    • PNG plots (unless --no-plots): histograms, violin plots, box plots, and composition pie/bar charts.
In short

It’s a post-processing aggregator for cosmic web topology analysis — taking per-voxel density classifications across many HDF5 crop outputs, pooling them, and producing publication-quality statistics and figures broken down by structure type (clusters, filaments, walls).

02:00:05Z — assistant

Given your sample sizes (tens of millions of points per category), a few things are worth keeping in mind before suggesting tests:

Important caveat: With this many observations, virtually every standard p-value test will return p≈0 regardless of whether the effect is scientifically meaningful. Effect size matters far more than significance here.

Most relevant tests for your data:

Distribution comparisons between categories - Two-sample KS test — compare the field_value distribution between pairs (e.g., walls_only vs clusters, filmans_not_clusters vs walls_and_filmans). Tells you if the distributions are drawn from the same underlying distribution - Anderson-Darling test — more sensitive than KS at the tails, relevant since cosmic density fields have heavy tails

Effect sizes (more meaningful than p-values here) - Cohen’s d — standardized difference in means between categories using your existing mean/std outputs - Overlap coefficient — what fraction of two distributions overlap, computable from your histograms

Distribution shape - Power-law / log-normal fit test — cosmic density fields are typically log-normal; you could test whether each category’s field_value distribution fits this, and compare the fit parameters (μ, σ) across categories

Structural overlap significance - Given your sigma-algebra structure, you could test whether shared_walls_filmans has a statistically distinct field_value distribution from walls_only or filmans_only — this would tell you whether co-membership in two structures has a measurable physical effect

All of these are computable from data you already have (histograms, means, stds, counts). Would you like me to add any of these to the script?

      def _quantile(vals_sorted: list[float], n: int, q: float) -> float:
    if n == 1:
        return float(vals_sorted[0])
    idx = q * (n - 1)
    lo = int(idx)
    hi = min(lo + 1, n - 1)
    frac = idx - lo
    return float(vals_sorted[lo] * (1 - frac) + vals_sorted[hi] * frac)

wall filman cluster →

F F T clusters
T F T clusters
F T T clusters
T T T clusters

That’s all intentional and correct.

02:21:03Z — user

You think the current method can be thougth of as density weighted mass distribution (given that the mass of each particle is 1)?

02:21:33Z — assistant

Not quite. Here’s why:

field_value at each point is the DTFE local density estimate (ρ_i), not a mass. If every particle has mass m = 1, then the actual mass in a category is simply its count — which is already what the first barchart shows. So the two charts would be identical under uniform mass.

What the current chart actually computes is:

proportion = Σ ρ_i  (over category)  /  Σ ρ_i  (over all points)

This is the fraction of the integrated density field in each structure, not density-weighted mass. It up-weights particles in dense regions — a single cluster particle contributes far more than a void particle. That’s a meaningful quantity (it answers “where is the density concentrated?”), but it’s distinct from mass distribution.

A true density-weighted mass proportion with uniform mass would be:

proportion = Σ (ρ_i × 1)  /  Σ (ρ_i × 1)  =  Σ ρ_i / Σ ρ_i

…which is the same thing. So the interpretation holds only if you define “effective mass” of a particle as its local density estimate, which isn’t the standard physical meaning.

In short: the current chart is better described as “fraction of integrated density field by structure type” rather than mass distribution. The chart title is misleading. Do you want to rename it, or change it to use the actual mass column?

The true_index IDs are local to each snapshot’s Delaunay tessellation — they’re not persistent Gadget particle IDs. The right approach is nearest-neighbor matching: for each particle in snapshot A, find the closest particle in snapshot B and treat it as the “same” one.

Using a chained approach (match 001→000, then 002→matched-001, etc.) is best because consecutive snapshots have minimal particle movement, making the matches accurate and physically meaningful.

What happens: before any rendering, the script builds a KD-tree on each snapshot and finds the nearest neighbor in the next snapshot for every point. Chaining means 000→001→002→003→004 — each step only needs to track small displacements. You’ll see log output like:

[info] Proximity-matching snapshot 1 (350000 ref pts → 350000 target pts) …
[info] Snapshot 1 matched.
...

If scipy is missing from your pvpython build, it falls back to positional order with a warning.

20:05:16Z — assistant

On persistent particle IDs: Yes — Gadget/Quijote HDF5 snapshots have a /PartType1/ParticleIDs array that is assigned once at the start of the simulation and never changes. The same physical particle has the same ID at z=3 and z=0. This is the correct way to track particles across redshifts.

The problem is that the true_index in the Delaunay VTU is not the Gadget particle ID — it’s the index DisPerSE assigns locally within its tessellation, recomputed fresh for each snapshot. To use Gadget IDs you’d need to go back to the original .hdf5 files, read ParticleIDs alongside coordinates, run the matching there, then re-export the VTUs — a significant pipeline change.

On compute cost of the current approach: For the crop you’re using (z900-1000, 500×500×100 volume), the point count is roughly ~175K — not 3.5M. A KDTree query on 175K points takes under a second per snapshot pair, so under 5 seconds total before rendering starts. Even for a full 3.5M point volume it would be ~1–2 minutes. Either way it’s not a bottleneck compared to the actual frame rendering.

Bottom line: just run it as-is. The proximity matching is fast and for a visualization it’s physically reasonable — in a cosmological simulation, the closest particle in the next snapshot is almost certainly the same physical particle (particles don’t “pass through” each other). The Gadget ID approach would be more rigorous but would require significant extra work for the same visual result.

    • ffmpeg concat demuxer: write a filelist.txt with file 'abs/path' + duration N entries; allows each image to be held for a specified duration without duplicate PNG frames. Absolute paths required.

        def _align_snapshots_by_proximity(snapshots):
    import time, numpy as np
    try:
        from scipy.spatial import cKDTree
    except ImportError:
        print("[warn] scipy not available — skipping proximity alignment (positional order).")
        return snapshots
    import scipy
    scipy_version = tuple(int(x) for x in scipy.__version__.split(".")[:2])
    use_workers = scipy_version >= (1, 6)
    aligned = [snapshots[0]]
    prev_coords = snapshots[0][0]
    for i, (coords, scalar, name) in enumerate(snapshots[1:], 1):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        tree = cKDTree(coords)
        t1 = time.perf_counter()
        if use_workers:
            _, idx = tree.query(prev_coords, k=1, workers=-1)
        else:
            _, idx = tree.query(prev_coords, k=1)
        t2 = time.perf_counter()
        matched_coords = coords[idx]
        matched_scalar = scalar[idx] if scalar is not None else None
        aligned.append((matched_coords, matched_scalar, name))
        prev_coords = matched_coords
        print(f"[info] Snapshot {i} matched — tree build {t1-t0:.1f}s, query {t2-t1:.1f}s, total {t2-t0:.1f}s")
    return aligned

        def _make_slideshow_mp4(frame_paths, args):
    concat_path = args.output_dir / f"{args.output_prefix}_concat.txt"
    with open(concat_path, "w") as f:
        for fp in frame_paths:
            abs_fp = Path(fp).resolve()
            f.write(f"file '{abs_fp}'\n")

  3. Errors and Fixes:

    • true_index not persistent across redshifts: user reported same ID maps to different particles. Root cause: true_index is DisPerSE’s local Delaunay index, not Gadget particle ID. Fix: replaced _align_snapshots_by_id() with _align_snapshots_by_proximity() using KDTree.
    • Concat demuxer path doubling (outputs/evolution_slideshow/outputs/evolution_slideshow/file.png): ffmpeg resolves relative paths relative to the concat file’s directory. Fix: use Path(fp).resolve() for absolute paths in concat file.
    • Double duration on last slideshow slide: trailing entry without duration caused ffmpeg to apply an implicit full duration. Fix: removed trailing duplicate entry entirely.
    • Label stuck in upper-left corner despite position change: ParaView’s Text annotation defaults WindowLocation to "UpperLeftCorner", overriding Position. Fix: set disp.WindowLocation = "Any Location" before setting disp.Position.
    • AnyLocation is not a valid value: ParaView 6.0.1 uses "Any Location" (with space). Error message said: AnyLocation is an obsolete value. Use Any Location instead. Fix: changed to "Any Location".
    • Changes not taking effect for user: user was running the correct script from the correct directory; root cause was that old output PNGs were being reused and the WindowLocation bug was preventing position changes from working.

  4. Problem Solving:

    • Particle tracking across redshifts: Codex/Gadget simulations have persistent ParticleIDs in the HDF5 files, but DisPerSE’s Delaunay VTUs use local indexing (true_index) that resets per snapshot. Proximity-based chained KDTree matching is the practical solution for visualization without modifying the upstream pipeline.
    • Slideshow efficiency: instead of generating N×hold_frames identical PNGs, render exactly N PNGs and encode duration into ffmpeg’s concat demuxer — much faster and avoids large output directories.
    • Sessions format unification: Codex and Claude Code have entirely different JSONL schemas. Auto-detection by filename pattern (rollout-* vs UUID format) dispatches to appropriate parsers. System context tags from Claude Code (<ide_opened_file> etc.) are stripped for readability.
